speechtext: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (weyburn) IN DEBATE ON MARCH 7

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) categorically denied a statement made by myself as to the policy of the C.C.F. party of British Columbia.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to have your ruling. First of all, on a question of privilege has the hon. member the right to deal with what was a question of fact? In the second place, if he is allowed to do that, am 1 permitted to reply to his statement, also on a question of privilege?

I am in this difficulty, that as yet I do not know what is the question of privilege. However, I would hope that
the hon. member who is raising the question would take into consideration what has been said by the hon. member for Weyburn.

I will state the question of privilege. The hon. member stated that I was quoting something from a newspaper, without having the newspaper here. A fair inference would be that I was stating to this house something that was incorrect as to the reported policy of his party in British Columbia. I claim the right to show this house that I was stating the situation correctly, and was not attempting to mislead the house by quoting from the newspaper to which I was referring.

I cannot agree that this is a question of privilege. Perhaps it could be brought up on the orders of the day, but certainly not as a question of privilege. If there is a dispute between two hon. members as to facts, there are other opportunities when they may make their statements.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO CANADA'S POSITION IN REGARD TO RECOGNITION OF NEW GOVERNMENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO CANADA'S POSITION IN REGARD TO RECOGNITION OF NEW GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked if I would make a statement with respect to the recognition or non-recognition of the present regime in Argentina. I have a statement to make which is a little longer than I might wish it to be. but I believe hon. members will appreciate having a statement given at some length.
The situation in Argentina' of recent months has caused considerable anxiety, both to her neighbours in the western hemisphere and to the united nations. This concern is provoked by the need for solidarity in the western hemisphere against axis intrigues and by the importance of Argentina as a source of foodstuffs and important raw materials for the united nations.
Since a coup d'etat overthrew the administration of President Castillo last June, the control of policies has passed from one military group to another, while the normal processes of democratic government have ceased to operate, parliament has not been summoned, political parties have been dissolved and the newspapers placed under more drastic controls. Within nine months, three generals have in turn exercised presidential powers, while the foreign office has been administered
Argentine Republic

by two admirals and two generals and, in addition, there have been several other cabinet changes.
On January 26 of this year the government of President Ramirez announced a rupture of diplomatic relations with the axis powers because of the revelation of axis intrigues within Argentina which were contrary to its neutrality and a threat to the security of the other American countries. This decision brought Argentina in line with the other countries of the western hemisphere, all of whom have either declared war upon Germany or severed diplomatic relations with her and other axis countries. The decision undoubtedly reflected the pro-allied sympathies of the great majority of the people of Argentina. It was thought to be a forerunner of other acts of hemispheric solidarity and defence.
In the month which followed, certain groups believed not to be in sympathy with the declared Argentine policy of joining the defence of the hemisphere were successful in forcing General Gilbert, Minister of Foreign Affairs to resign on February 15. Ten days later they secured the delegation of the powers of General Ramirez as president to the vicepresident and minister of war, General Farrell.
Following these changes in personnel the United States government instructed its ambassador, Mr. Norman Armour "to refrain from entering into official relations with the new regime pending developments." A statement describing the reasons for the position taken by the United States was issued by Mr. Stettinius, acting Secretary of State, on March 4, which stressed the fact that in Argentina "the support by important elements inimical to the united nations war effort of movements designed to eliminate action already taken could only be a matter of grave anxiety."
In response to a question in the British House of Commons yesterday, the British foreign secretary stated that in view of the obscurity surrounding the circumstances of President Ramirez' delegation of his function to Vice-President Farrell, the British ambassador in Argentina had confined his communications with the Argentine government to routine matters only. The same position had been taken as regards communications between the British government and the Argentine ambassador in London. Mr. Eden also announced that this attitude would be maintained pending developments in Buenos Aires.
The Canadian government has been kept fully informed of developments in Argentina by its legation in Buenos Aires. It has also had the benefit of first hand information from the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, who only recently

returned from serving as minister in Argentina. Pending a clarification of what remains a most confused and obscure situation, the government has instructed the Canadian charge d'affaires in Buenos Aires to refrain for the present from any official contacts with the administration of General Farrell. With the people of Argentina our friendship remains unaffected. We hope and trust that Argentina will evolve a policy commensurate with her past, worthy of her citizens and calculated to meet the needs of hemispheric defence.

speechtext:
On Tuesday last the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to documents which had been tabled concerning relations before the war between Japanese interests and the Granby Mining Corporation. My hon. friend quoted a statement made by the Japanese minister in a letter dated October 22, 1940, to the effect that the contract of the Granby company with the Japanese company had been approved by the Canadian government and added that he could find in the return no document relating to the contract or to approval by the government. I informed the hon. member that my recollection was that the government had had nothing to do with the contract and that I believed this was made clear in the correspondence.
I have now had an opportunity to have the matter checked and I find that my original impression was correct. In the reply dated November 22, 1940, from the Department of External Affairs to the Japanese minister is the following paragraph, and which I should say was in the return which my hon. friend had:
In this connection it should be clearly understood that the contract between the Granby Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for the sale of its output of copper concentrates to a Japanese purchaser had never been "approved by the Canadian government." So far as the Canadian government was concerned, this arrangement was an ordinary private commercial contract which did not require or receive the approval or disapproval of the Canadian government.
The correspondence itself shows how the idea first gained currency that the Canadian government had given its approval. After the fact was pointed out to the Japanese minister that the contract was a purely commercial transaction which had not been given the approval of the government, the Japanese minister admitted that he had never seen any confirmation of the approval, and added:

Granby Mining Corporation
Pending further instructions from my government, I desire to say with reference to the above, that the intimation I made in our memorandum of the 22nd ultimo to the effect that this sale of copper had been carried on with the approval of the Canadian government had its basis in a passage of the speech Mr. M. J. Coldwell delivered in the House of Commons on July 31, 1940.
This is contained in a letter of November 30, 1940, which is included in the return tabled.
The hon. member referred to the Granby Mining Corporation on three occasions in 1940, and it was really on May 20, at page 53 of Hansard, that he claimed that "the contract was made with the approval of the government," although he did refer to the matter again on July 31.
To conclude this question, I wish merely to point out that the Granby contract was entered into in January, 1940, almost two years before Japan entered the war. It was a commercial contract which the government was not called upon to approve or disapprove. However, as the final item of the correspondence, a letter of December 4, 1940, from Doctor .
O.	D. Skelton to the Japanese minister, makes clear:
Like all such contracts, its performance was subject to the general conditions of the public interest, and it ceased to be binding when the copper requirements of Canada and her allies compelled the Canadian government to withhold further permits for the export of copper from Canada to other countries.

short fibre asbestos and asbestos waste used for making building materials.
All shipments to Spain must pass through the allied blockade and must therefore be cleared through the blockade controls. subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO REFERENCE TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO REFERENCE TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
I should like to make a
statement with reference to matters pertaining to the Columbia river which have been referred for investigation to the international joint commission. I am making the statement now because it has been agreed that it will be made simultaneously at Washington.
The governments of Canada and the United States have agreed to refer to the international joint commission, for investigation and report, the question whether it would be feasible and advantageous to make a greater use than is now being made of the waters of the Columbia river system. The reference to the commission is being made under article IX of the treaty relating to boundary waters between the United States and Canada, signed on January 11, 1909.
As questions concerning the Columbia river basin are of great interest to the province of British Columbia, the government of that province has been consulted at all stages in the drafting of this reference.
The report of the international joint commission will not be binding on the governments concerned, but it is likely that the investigations of the commission will result in suggestions and recommendations which will be carried into effect by joint action of the two governments.
The commission has to date dealt with nine separate applications with reference to specific problems concerning the Columbia river and its tributaries. The present reference concerns the entire Columbia river system. It is based on the realization that a large part of the water resources of the two countries in this important river basin is being allowed1 to go to waste because of lack of adequate regulation and control, and upon the desirability of more effective flood control. The investigation by the commission will cover domestic water supply and sanitation, navigation, efficient development of water power, the control of

floods, the needs of irrigation, the reclamation of wet lands, the conservation of wild life and other beneficial public purposes.
When the commission has completed its investigations there will be available to the two governments a complete and detailed report on the best uses to which the waters of this vast river basin can be put.
The Columbia river is 1,200 miles long. In comparison, the St. Lawrence from Duluth to Father Point is 1,700 miles long. The watershed of the Columbia river is 259,000 square miles, of which 39,400 are in Canada.
At present there is a total installed capacity of approximately 450,000 horse-power in the Columbia river basin in Canada. The studies to be undertaken by the commission will determine the total potential water power in the basin.
The Columbia is a truly international river. Any development, and particularly any power development, of the resources of the river on one side of the boundary is certain to have an effect in the other country. For this reason it is necessary that the plans for development of the river basin in one country should be adapted to those in the other.
It is unlikely that a complete report by the commission will be available for several years, but it is expected that the commission will bring out interim reports from time to time with regard to projects which might be integrated with post-war rehabilitation plans.
I now table for the information of the house copies in English and French of the reference by the Canadian government to the international joint commission.

1.	Were charges made in a circular dated November 16, 1943, addressed to members of parliament, municipal officials and others by J. W. Gilbert, Hanover, Ontario, that employers had taken advantage of compulsory labour transfer orders of national selective service, to reduce wages?
2.	If so, was an investigation made into the charges?
3.	What was the result of such investigation?

1.	Yes. Mr. Gilbert made two complaints concerning the administration of the national selective service civilian regulations.-
(1)	That, under the compulsory employment transfer orders, married men engaged in non-essential work were directed by the employment and selective service office, Walkerton, Ont., to apply for and accept essential employment at lower wage rates;
(2)	That a certain employer in Hanover, Ont., (later identified as William Knech-tel & Son, Limited) had "taken advantage of the compulsory selective service transfer of employees from nonessential work to lower his pay .for beginners" from 36c per hour (cost of living bonus included) in September, to 31c per hour (cost of living bonus included) in November, 1943.
2.	Yes, a very complete investigation.
3.	The result of the investigation indicated that Mr. Gilbert based his complaints on mere hearsay without making any attempt to verify

the information or to secure an understanding of the national selective service civilian regulations involved.	i
With regard to the first complaint, only one married man was directed to and ordered to accept employment by the employment and selective service office at Walkerton under the compulsory employment transfer orders. This man was not directed to the William Kneehtel & Son, Limited, of Hanover, referred to in the second complaint. Furthermore, this man, upon being directed under the compulsory employment orders, received a wage rate of 3c per hour more from the employer to whom he was directed than he did from his former employer. In addition to this, he was directed to employment where he was able to work a greater number of hours per week than he had been working in his original employment. The charge with respect to the transfer of married men is, therefore, unsubstantiated.
In answer to the second complaint, no persons, either single or married, have been directed to employment with the Kneehtel & Son, Limited, referred to. It is true that a number of men have been referred to this employer in accordance with the national selective service civilian regulations. Regarding the rate of wages paid by this firm, the records indicate that from August 1 to the present time every new employee hired received an initial wage rate of 30c per hour, plus 60c per week cost of living bonus. It is wholly untrue and contrary to the facts that the administration of the national selective service civilian regulations made it possible for this employer to lower the wage rate being paid to new employees.

On the orders of the day:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Following the precedent set last
year by my hon. and esteemed friend the member for Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt) when he mentioned' the decoration that had been awarded to Lieutenant-Colonel C. C. Merritt, V.C., after the Dieppe raid, it is my privilege to-day, sir, to mention again to the house the signal honour which has been bestowed on Major Paul Triquet, V.C., of Cabano, Temis-couata, P.Q. In the whole world there is a feeling of admiration for the hero, and we of the united nations take, special pride in recalling that he is the second Canadian to receive such a coveted decoration from the hands of His Majesty during this war.
Very often, in the schools, young people are told of Leonidas at Thermopylae. They should be taught modern history. If they are told about Leonidas, they should know also of Merritt and Menard at Dieppe, of Triquet at Casa Berardi in Italy, and all the heroes of our time who have been awarded decorations for their gallantry. That should be done by way of recognition of what these men have achieved, and in recognition as well of the unknown soldier.
I have two suggestions to offer. The first is that all citations giving the reasons why awards for gallantry have been granted should be sorted, and if all citations are not sent to each school, at least the citations regarding the men of each constituency should be sent to each school of that constituency in order to inform young children of what has been done by gallant Canadians during this war.
My other suggestion is a very practical one, and here again we have the example of Westminster in the matter of parliamentary grants which were awarded to Nelson, to Wellington and to all the great leaders of the navy and of the army. Moreover, we have the example set by this parlaiment, with regard to Sir Arthur Currie. In my humble view there should be a tax-free parliamentary grant to each living holder of the V.C. which would enable him to live independently.
I submit these suggestions, sir, and I take this opportunity to congratulate the family of Major Paul Triquet, V.C., on the signal honour which has been conferred upon him and which is shared by all his men.

The remarks of the hon.
member have raised a question in my mind. All hon. members of this house will probably in the future find themselves in the same position as the hon. gentleman, in that they will wish to call attention to the bravery, and the consequent decoration, of men in their respective constituencies. If the precedent that is set to-day is not followed on subsequent occasions I shall perhaps be in the position of having to differentiate between hon. members. I should like therefore to have the sense of the house in the matter. My own opinion is that the government should of itself do the proposed honours to soldiers who may be decorated for having distinguished themselves in the war, and that this should be sufficient for the house. Otherwise I shall be faced with this question throughout the session.

At such a time as this one is tempted to !Mr. Speaker.]
look back into other years and to compare the general situation of to-day with the conditions of other times. In 1941, when I first presented the estimates of this department to the house, the general position of our arms was highly precarious. The British commonwealth stood alone, the battle of Britain etill raged, air assaults of great fierceness and magnitude had been launched against that

War Appropriation-Naval Services
island; and even as I spoke three years ago her cities, her factories, her ports, yes, her ancient monuments even were being subjected to heavy and bitter attack from the air. The battle of the Atlantic, or the campaign of the Atlantic as it should more properly be called, was s,till in a most critical and indecisive stage, and the island fortress of Britain, whose very existence depended on the successful issue of that struggle, was threatened with disaster. Only a few months before, Mr. Churchill said, in a passage remarkable, even among Churehillian utterances, for its eloquent beauty:
And now it has come to us to stand alone in the breach, and face the worst that the tyrant's might and enmity can do. Bearing ourselves humbly before God, but conscious that we serve an unfolding purpose, we are ready to defend our native land. We are fighting by ourselves alone; but we are not fighting for ourselves alone. Here, in this strong city of refuge which enshrines the title deeds of human progress and is of deep consequence to Christian civilization; here, girt about by the seas and oceans where the navy reigns; shielded from above by the prowess and devotion of our airmen-we await undismayed the impending assault.
By 1942 the forces of the British commonwealth had been joined by the great armed strength of Russia and the United States; but, on the other hand, the formidable fleets and armies of Japan had been ranged against us.
The struggle on the Atlantic assumed a more direct and sinister form for us in Canada when, in that same year, German submarines penetrated into the gulf and lower reaches of the St. Lawrence and there sank merchant ships and warships.
The year 1943 began with loudly-voiced and widely heralded threats by the new supreme commander of the German navy, Admiral Doenitz, an officer of very considerable submarine experience, who spoke confidently of new weapons and plans of attack which would disrupt our sea communications with Europe, and inflict great losses on our ships of war. But the predictions of Admiral Doenitz still stand in the realm of unfulfilled prophecy rather than in the world of solid achievement. The year that has passed marked the most successful defence ever made by our ships of war, both surface ships and air, against the attacks of submarines; and it saw the greatest number of submarine destructions ever recorded in a similar ' period. The Atlantic campaign is not yet won, but no one can deny that the tide of that campaign turned definitely in our favour during the year.
U-boat destruction. Well over two hundred enemy U-boats were destroyed in 1943, most 100-83J
of them German, hut some of them Japanese and some of them Italian. In the war of 1914 to 1918 the total number of enemy submarines destroyed was just short of two hundred. Thus in the year 1943 alone the destruction of enemy submarines was greater than in the whole period of the last great war. This destruction of U-boats is of twofold beneficial effect to us. Every U-boat destroyed takes with it either to the bottom of the sea or as prisoners on allied warships the skilled enemy captains and officers on whose training and courage so much of the success of U-boat warfare depends. It also deprives the enemy of one more weapon to be used in his war against our shipping.
I come now to a point which I think is deserving of mention. In 1942, as I have said, German U-boats ranged far afield and reached the coastal waters of Canada. There immediately arose in certain quarters of this country loud demands for the redisposition of the Canadian navy. There were those who urged that the Canadian navy should be disposed in the Cabot strait, in the strait of Belle Isle :md in the gulf of St. Lawrence, there to await submarine attacks. Under this arrangement, of course, we would have to rely on some other navy to protect those ships, our own Canadian ships and ships of allied nations, while they were carrying Canadian food and Canadian war supplies on the high seas. Nevertheless that was the arrangement that certain people in this country wished to see put into effect.
Those responsible for our naval strategy however held strongly to the view that while we should give protection to our own shores and coastal waters, and while certain ships, should be maintained in those localities for that purpose, nevertheless Canadian ships of war operating anywhere on the Atlantic were a protection not only to our shipping but to our shores as well. And so the Canadian navy went on with its assistance in the great work of convoying allied merchant ships and attacking enemy submarines wherever such attacks presented themselves.
In the year 1943 not a single German submarine made an attack in the gulf or river St. Lawrence. The reason for the immunity which we enjoyed last year is to be found. I think, in the fact that Canadian and allied warships and planes met and attacked the U-boats far out in the Atlantic, and those under-sea marauders had little opportunity of making attacks close to our coasts.
The Atlantic campaign has gone much more successfully in the past year than in previous years, but it is a mistake, a great mistake.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
to think that it has been won. I have always held the view that no matter what may happen in any other theatre of war Germany must continue her attacks on our shipping to the end. She may be driven out of Africa or out of Sicily and yet she can continue to fight on strongly. But when it comes to pass that Germany lacks the strength or the inclination to attack our shipping, then we shall know that she is ready to throw in her hand. For she knows of a certainty how important, how vital is the line between these shores and Europe, and one of her greatest hopes for victory must lie in the breaking or disruption of that line.
The Atlantic campaign has gone well for us because of the increased strength of allied naval and air forces in that ocean and because of the effective cooperation between these forces. Shore based aircraft, carrier based aircraft, have proved to be most important factors in this struggle, not alone because of their own striking power but also because of their ability to detect and report the presence of enemy underwater craft.
Shipbuilding. I come now to the question of shipbuilding, and I shall show that the increased strength of allied naval forces'comes as a result of the magnificent efforts made by the managers and workers in the shipyards of the allied nations. Despite losses, the service navies of Great Britain, the United States and Canada are definitely and decidedly greater in strength than they were at the beginning of the war. All losses of fighting ships have been more than replaced.
In a few moments I shall come to deal with the production of warships in Canadian yards, but I may say at this moment that by far the greater number, indeed almost the entire number, of our fighting ships have been built in Canadian yards by Canadian workmen out of Canadian materials. When war broke out the shipbuilding industry in Canada could be described as virtually non-existent. A few shipyards existed on our east and west coasts and on the shores of our great lakes and on the river St. Lawrence; but they had become mainly ship repair yards, and probably there were not five thousand men in all Canada in the shipbuilding and ship repair industry. From these small beginnings the Department of Munitions and Supply has succeeded in developing a shipbuilding industry whose efforts have amazed the world. So far as ships of war are concerned, at first we had to import much of the material required, much of the steel for the hulls, the auxiliary machinery and other apparatus necessary for the equipment and operation of ships of war. [Mr. A. L. Macdonald.)
Probably it would be true to say that our first ships were not more than 50 per cent Canadian manufacture. But we have advanced far beyond that stage of. dependence upon other countries. To-day the ships of war building in Canadian yards, in their material, their machinery, their guns and other equipment, are about 95 per cent a Canadian product. These figures, I think, speak eloquently of the successful efforts of Canadian factories, Canadian management, Canadian workmen and Canadian shipyards.
But that is not all; we have done more than build ships of war for ourselves. We have built already not far from 100 ships of war for the British Navy, and we have now building in Canadian yards or on order in those yards about the same number of ships for that great navy. We have built also a few ships of war for the United States Navy.
In the realm of merchant shipping, United States, British and Canadian yards are now and for some time have been turning out merchant ships at a rate much faster than the rate at which they are being sunk, the United States of course supplying the greater share of that tonnage. There would now seem to be every justification for the statement that we can maintain this ratio against the worst the enemy can do. We can continue to produce merchant ships faster than he can sink them. Thus both offensively and defensively the story of the sea is much brighter at this time than in previous years.
Growth of navy. Now, Mr. Chairman, let me continue in historical vein for a moment longer and give the committee some figures to illustrate the growth of the Canadian navy. I have been looking at a report recently prepared by the naval staff showing the development of the Canadian navy since the beginning of the war, and it presents a story of truly remarkable expansion. The 6 combat ships we had at the beginning of the war have grown to roughly 250 fighting ships. The auxiliary vessels and patrol craft, which numbered 7 in the early days of September, 1939, now stand at more than 450. So that the number of our ships has increased more than fifty-fold1 in a little over four years. When war broke out we had not quite 1,800 men on active service in the Canadian navy. To-day Canadian naval personnel number approximately 80,000, which is a forty-fivefold increase.
In September, 1939, we had only two naval bases, one at Halifax on the east coast and the other at Esquimalt on the west. To-day those two bases have been greatly expanded and im-

War Appropriation-Naval Services
proved, and in addition eleven new bases have been developed on our eastern and western coasts and in Newfoundland.
These developments have involved not merely the construction of buildings where men can be housed and trained and fedi, but also the construction of all the other facilities necessary for a naval base, such as docks, wharves, repair shops, marine railways and the like. Since the beginning of the war we have put into operation at one of our bases a great floating dock capable of taking ships of as great a tonnage as 25,000. We have constructed three marine railways at various points capable of carrying for repairs the largest destroyer, and another similar marine railway is building. We have built three smaller marine railways that can take corvettes and minesweepers. In addition we have built and have in operation three still smaller marine railways, and four more are building, where the lighter types of craft such as Fairmile motor launches and other vessels of that general size can 'be taken in hand for repair.
At the beginning of the war, the Canadian Navy did not own a single bit of land in the great space between Halifax and Victoria. The volunteer reserve divisions, which were first instituted in 1923 during the regime of Commodore Hose as chief of naval staff, under the provisions of the Naval Service Act of 1910, were living in rented quarters, some of which were totally inadequate for the purpose. We have changed a good deal of that. Most of these divisions have now been established in buildings of their own. In some cases we have bought buildings and renovated them to suit our purposes. In other instances we constructed new buildings, where naval ratings have the advantage of living, eating and being trained in proper 'barracks. The work of improving the facilities of these volunteer reserve divisions is still going on; for we at naval service headquarters realize that without these divisions at the beginning of the war, and without the work they have done since in recruiting' men and supervising their preliminary training, it would not have been possible for us to achieve what we h.-ve achieved in the four years of war.
The committee perhaps will be more interested in later events and developments, and I propose now to give to the committee some figures to Indicate what we have succeeded in accomplishing in the last fourteen months or since January 1, 1943. In that time we have added approximately 27,000 to the personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy. At January 1, 1943, we had a total complement
of approximately 53,000. To-day we have a total complement of approximately 80,000. The personnel of the Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service has increased from about
1,000	at January 1, 1943, to 4,500 to-day. These Wrens, as they are commonly called, are serving at thirty-two different points in Canada as well as in the United States, Newfoundland and Canada. This service has in every way justified its existence; and the attitude of its members towards their work, as well as their behaviour when off duty, I think have won general and well-deserved praise.
Questions have been asked in the house as to enlistments by provinces, and if I may I should like to place upon Hansard a table showing enlistments in the naval service by provinces complete as at December 31, 1943. Perhaps I need not read the figures, if the committee will allow me to place them on Hansard. About forty per cent of our men are serving at sea at the present time; a large number of those on shore have had sea service. Others ashore are undergoing training or carrying on administrative, instructional or professional duties.

Training. Next comes the question of training. One of the great problems in a navy which has grown as quickly as ours is that of training. Many thousands of young men have been taken into the service since the beginning of the war and many of them had no knowledge whatever of ships or of the equipment which makes a warship effective. It is not enough that a man in the navy be a good sailor in the old sense. Warfare to-day in the air, on land and at sea involves the operation of technical gear, and in order to conduct this warfare successfully great attention must be paid to training.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
In general, naval training is divided into two main categories. The first is the basic or new entry training which is given to the new [DOT]recruits, and the second is the advanced or technical training which is provided for men who have had some experience at sea in ships. The initial stages of the new entry training take place at the reserve divisions throughout the country and those stages are completed at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis at Deep Brook, Nova Scotia.
At the beginning of last year the service was deficient in facilities for advanced technical training. I have said already that as of January 1, 1943, there were approximately 53,000 personnel in the Royal Canadian Navy. There was bound to be a great backlog of men with some sea time who had not had the opportunity of qualifying for promotion to higher rank. The opening of the training establishment H.M.C.S. Cornwallis -has solved, or at any rate has helped1 to solve, this serious problem. Despite the difficulties of securing equipment and despite all the other problems incidental to the opening of so large an establishment, over 16,000 ratings have been given courses of one kind and another at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis in less than a year. I cannot emphasize too strongly what this institution has meant in the way of improving the fighting efficiency of our ships.
Some idea of the value of this establishment can be gained when I say that the number of men who have been trained for higher duties of a technical nature at this establishment in less than nine months in 1943 was almost as great as the total number trained from the beginning of the war until the opening of this establishment.
The removal from Halifax of this training establishment where the great bulk of the naval training ashore, both technical and new entry, is conducted, has had many advantages. The morale of the men has been improved by the provision of better training facilities with ample time under naval discipline. The removal of
6,500	men from Halifax to Deep Brook has allowed for the further expansion of repair facilities for ships at Halifax. The proximity of Deep Brook to Halifax permits of a free and fast flow of men to and from ships.
If one thousand men are brought from ships to Cornwallis or from Cornwallis to ships, in order that they may take courses or report back to their ships after completing courses, the question of distance becomes very important and the need of having Cornwallis within easy reach of our main naval base is readily apparent.
(Mr. A. L. Macdonald.]
Many of the men who joined the navy have learned trades which I hope they can put to use when they return to civilian life. In addition to' those trained in the naval establishments, of whom there are a very large number, I may tell the committee that approximately 4,400 ratings have been trained in civilian schools since the outbreak of the war in such work as plumbing, electrical work, radio artificer work, internal combustion engine work, welding, copper-smithing, boiler making, machine shop work and the like. In addition more than 1,000 are at present undergoing such training in civilian schools at Halifax, Fredericton, Kingston, Toronto, Hamilton, Galt, Windsor, Calgary and Edmonton.
University Naval Training College. Now a word about the university naval training divisions. Fifteen Canadian universities are participating in the university naval training scheme. The initial enrolments took place in the spring of 1943 and there have been over
1,500	entries. Of those entries 150 have been taken on active service as ratings, thirty-eight have been discharged and there remain in the universities a total of some 1,200 men. More than 250 of these will go on active service at the end of the present school term. The training of the university students is conducted during the academic year at the universities. In the summer time the trainees all put in a special course of two weeks, either at H.M.C.S. Cornv)allis on the east coast or at Esquimalt in British Columbia.
Naval College. The Royal Canadian Naval College was opened at Royal Roads, British Columbia, on October 21, 1942. In the first term 100 students were enrolled, fifty for a one-year course and fifty for a two-year course. In the spring of 1943 forty-three midshipmen were graduated. Of this number, 27 have been selected for permanent membership in the Royal Canadian Navy and they are now serving as midshipmen in large ships of the Royal Navy., The other 16 of the graduating class joined the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve and are serving at sea as midshipmen on Canadian ships. All R.C.N.V.R. graduates who have served six months at sea and who have reached the age of nineteen years with satisfactory service will be promoted to the rank of sub-lieutenant, R.C.N.V.R. Midshipmen who are members of the permanent force must serve eighteen months as midshipmen before they can qualify as sub-lieutenants in the permanent force. It is a pleasure to tell the committee that I have heard nothing but favourable comment on the work of this college. Its staff has been carefully

War Appropriation-Naval Services
selected. Its scholastic standard is high, and its discipline and training are in themselves valuable factors in a boy's education.
Teaching of English. In the fall of 1943, the school for instruction of French-speaking Canadians in English was transferred from H.M.CJ3. Montcalm in Quebec, to H.M.C.S. Prevost, in London, Canada. Classroom space has been provided in the public library at London. The course lasts some three months and most of the work done there is in English. Trainees are billeted in homes in the city of London. To date there has been nothing but the most favourable of reports on the work done at'the school and on the kindness shown by the citizens of that city.
Entry of officers.-We have made some changes as to the entry of officers. All new officers in the Executive (combatant) branch must enter the service as ordinary seamen and serve on the lower deck. If any of these men aspire to a commission they may request of their commanding officer to be so considered. Upon his recommendation and upon passing a selection board they then qualify for a short selection course at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis which culminates in an appearance before the permanent promotion board. Success means a commission as probationary sub-lieutenant, and in due course, entry to King's college for the prescribed four months officers' training course there.
When an officer has passed out of King's, however, he has not finished his training by any means. His real diploma as an officer is, in fact, his watehkeeping certificate. This he can only acquire after approximately six months' service at sea. Even then officers must constantly requalify and take additional courses, both in our own schools and in the training schools of the Royal Navy. New methods of sea w-arfare, new equipment, are constantly being developed and our seagoing officers must keep up with these ever-changing situations devised either by the ingenuity of our own scientists or by the resourcefulness of a ruthless enemy.
Operations. As I pointed out last year our men are serving on every sea of the world, in the Atlantic, in the Pacific, in the Mediterranean, in the Indian ocean, in the cold of Arctic waters, and in the balmier seas of the south.
Last year seventeen Ganadian corvettes took part in the Mediterranean campaign when North Africa was wrested from the enemy. Sea power played a large part in this great achievement and Canadian corvettes definitely destroyed three submarines in the Mediterranean. In the early part of last year six of our corvettes and a flotilla of motor launches
saw duty in the Caribbean area. Canadian ships of war participated in the Aleutian Islands campaign of last year, and I am glad to be able to say that their work was made the subject of a laudatory letter from the senior United States naval officer who was in charge of the operation.
' In July, when Sicily was invaded, four Canadian flotillas of landing craft took part in the operation.
In September, when the invasion of the mainland of Italy began, the same four Canadian flotillas were on duty in the straits of Messina, and I am proud to report that the services which they performed were such as to win the praise of senior British naval officers.
As was announced in September, 1943, a minesweeping operation of considerable magnitude was conducted off the port of Halifax. The mines almost undoubtedly were laid by an enemy submarine which, instead of attacking ships directly, chose to lay mines in the path of convoys. A considerable number of enemy mines were detected in the area and our minesweepers cleared them up rapidly, and made safe the ocean exit from that great harbour. I should like to repeat now what I said at the time by way of appreciation of and praise for the men of the Canadian navy, who, day in and day out, sweep certain portions of the convoy channel for mines. The work is tedious, but nevertheless it is important and necessary. No lives were lost from these mines, though one ship, a convoy straggler which strayed from the channel which had been swept, struck a mine and was destroyed.
I may mention for the information of the committee that our Tribal destroyers, which are the newest and fastest destroyers in the world, have seen service with convoys to north Russia. As is appreciated, because of the threat held out to these convoys by enemy warships based in Norwegian waters, and because of the great vulnerability of that sea route to intensive bombing from northern European bases, a heavier type of protection must be provided there than is normally required on the north Atlantic. Canadian Tribals were with the attacked convoys off Bear island when the Schamhorst was torpedoed' on December 26, 1943.
During the summer and early fall, the Tribal destroyer H.M.C.S. Athabaskan was engaged in offensive operational work in the bay of Biscay. It is worthy of record to say that she was the first ship to be attacked by the newly-developed German aerial bomb. She sustained considerable damage in that action. I should add that her commanding officer, Captain

War Appropriation-Naval Services
G.	R. Miles, R.C.N., succeeded in trying and hazardous conditions in bringing his crippled ship safely to port. This was the second time Captain Miles performed such a feat. In December of 1940 he was in command of
H.	M.C.S. Saguenay when she was torpedoed in the north Atlantic, and after many hours on her bridge, eventually he made her fast alongside at a British' port, where she was repaired, and went to sea again to continue her work in the Atlantic campaign against the submarine.
Convoys. Our main work during the year consisted, as in the past, of escorting merchant ships in the north Atlantic.
A few moments ago I pointed out that the destruction of enemy submarines had been very great during the year. That is one way of estimating the success of our battle against U-boats. I believe that the success of that battle was one of the outstanding features of the whole war during the year, but, as I pointed out earlier, it must not be supposed that the battle is over. Germany still has a great many U-boats and there is no reason whatever to think that she will not use them to the utmost in attacks against allied shipping.
The destruction of U-boats is one way of measuring the success of our convoy efforts. Another way is to consider the number of merchant ships that get safely through. Speaking in the British House of Commons on Tuesday of this week, the Hon. Mr. Alexander, First Lord of the Admiralty, pointed out that in 1941, one ship was lost out of every 181 that sailed; in 1942, one out of every 233, while in 1943 only one out of every 344 was lost. In other words, the proportion of ships getting through safely in 1943 was nearly twice as great as in 1941.	\
Mr. Alexander was giving here figures for all allied ships. He includes the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Mediterranean route, the Russian route, and every other ocean lane on which allied ships operate. The Canadian navy has operated in many waters, but its special area is the north Atlantic over which must pass the supplies produced in Canada and the United States, which must be safely transported to the shores of the British isles.
On this route we have at times supplied 48 per cent of the convoy escort, and during the past two years I think it can be safely said that we have never done less than 40 per cent of the convoy escort work. From the beginning of the war up to the end of 1943 the Canadian navy has escorted, or assisted in escorting, more than 18,000 ships from North America to Europe, and about 114

million dead-weight tons of shipping has safely made this perilous crossing.
One hundred and fourteen million tons of food, of war supplies of all kinds so vital to the efforts of our allies in the European theatre of war have reached their destination and more than 40 per cent of the credit must go to the navy of Canada, which began the war with only six ships capable of undertaking escort work. Is there in the history of all warfare a record more heroic and more inspiring? Young Canadians from our eastern and western ocean gateways, young Canadians from the shores of the St. Lawrence and the great lakes, and, what is even more remarkable, Canadians from the three prairie provinces, many of whom never saw the sea until after the outbreak of war-all have banded together to write one of the most romantic and remarkable stories in the history of naval warfare.
In addition to the ships convoyed from American shores to Europe, our navy has also assisted in the convoying of some 10,000 ships from United Kingdom ports to ports on this continent.
Furthermore, some 20,000 ships have sailed in Canadian coastal convoys so-called, that is to say, from some point on the North American continent to another point in the same area, and almost the entire task of convoy protection in this area has fallen upon the ships and men of the Canadian navy.
If you add all these figures together you will find that nearly 50,000 ships in one way or another have come under the protection of the Canadian navy.
It is in the north Atlantic that the fiercest efforts of German submarines are put forth. There lies the lifeline which in this war, as in the last, the enemy must endeavour to snap. That line has been subjected to many strains and stresses, but it still holds. The supplies are still going through, and not only the supplies, but the ships carrying men, Canadians and Americans, men of all services, are plying the north Atlantic route.
I cannot go into all the details of losses in transatlantic convoys since the beginning of the war, but I can say that the last six months of 1943 showed a remarkable improvement over any previous similar period since the outbreak of war. But as Mr. Alexander pointed out on Tuesday, the German submarine strength is still as great as it was at the beginning of 1943, and we have no assurance whatever that that strength will not again be unleashed against transatlantic shipping. Nor is there any guarantee that we shall not yet have to face attacks on shipping in our own coastal zones.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Losses. You cannot undertake operations of the magnitude which I have briefly described' without suffering some losses. Since the 1st of January, 1943, we have lost four ships of war. The corvettes Louisburg and Weyburn were lost in the North African operations. The minesweeper Chedabucto was lost as the result of a collision with a merchant ship, and the destroyer St. Croix was lost as the result of enemy action in the autumn of last year. The St. Croix was one of the seven destroyers acquired by us from the United States in 1940, and I should like to say now that all these seven ships have been of the greatest value and benefit to us. The St. Croix was hit by enemy torpedoes, and sank, carrying with her more than half of her crew. The rest of the crew succeeded in getting aboard a British frigate, but, unfortunately, on the following night the frigate herself was torpedoed and all the survivors of the St. Croix, with one exception, went to their death. The sinking of the St. Croix marked the heaviest single loss that the Canadian navy has yet received.
Destruction of submarines. We have lost four ships, but we have had revenge. The Canadian Navy since the 1st of January, 1943, has had a hand in the definite and certain destruction of eight submarines, and in the probable or possible sinking or damaging of seven other submarines.
Of the eight submarines definitely destroyed four were sent to the bottom of the sea by Canadian ships alone. Three were destroyed by Canadian ships cooperating with British ships; and one by a Canadian ship working with a Royal Canadian Air Force plane and a British ship-of-war.
Additions to ship strength. In the past fourteen months we have added some seventy fighting ships to our navy, destroyers, frigates, corvettes, minesweepers and Fairmile motor launches. We have added two more Tribal destroyers, namely the Huron and Haida to our fleet. We have also acquired eight other destroyers from the British admiralty.
Casualties. Our casualties since the beginning of the war in dead, wounded, missing and prisoners now stand at more than 1,300. I know that the house will join with me in paying tribute to those naval officers and ratings who have died in their country's service; and in tendering deepest sympathy to their relatives and friends. Their lives have been a source of inspiration. Their deaths have been models of gallantry and courage.
Decorations. The heroism and devotion of our officers and ratings has been recognized no fewer than 513 times by decorations and mentions in dispatches. Within a day or two, I
shall place on Hansard a statement showing the names and addresses of all those who have been thus honoured.
Navy League and Sea Cadets. The members of the committee have always been interested in the sea cadet movement. Personally,
I have always tried to encourage the great work which is being done in this respect by the Navy League of Canada, and I am only too happy tb repeat the tribute which I have on past occasions paid to that organization for their work not only in connection with sea cadets, but also in connection with hostels for merchant seamen, and for other welfare work undertaken by them on behalf of those people who are engaged in the war at sea.
On the 31st of December, 1943, there were eighty-six Canadian sea cadet corps and over 13,700 cadets enrolled. When the naval service assumed some of the responsibility for the training of sea cadets in 1941, there were some twenty-three corps in Canada with an enrolment of 2,300 cadets. Just now six new corps are being organized, and it is expected that very soon the authorized complement of
15,000	sea cadets will be reached.
More than 5,000 former sea cadets are now in the naval service. Accurate figures for enlistments have been kept for the past eight months ,and they indicate that while all the forces are attracting members of the sea cadet corps, the navy seems to be the favoured service for these boys.
The figures for enlistments in the past eight months are: Navy, 5S1; army, SO; air force, 66; merchant navy, 63.
Apart altogether from the value which this work has for the naval service, most satisfactory *reports have been received to the effect that the work of the sea cadets corps-and I am sure this is true of the air cadet corps and the army cadets as well-has had a very considerable influence in reducing the number of cases of juvenile delinquency in the centres where cadet work is carried out.
There are over 750 men serving as sea cadet officers in the various corps. They are public spirited citizens who give freely of their time and who have made a great contribution to the success of the sea cadet movement. They have helped greatly to inculcate high ideals of citizenship in these young boys.
In the summer of 1943 the naval service sponsored thirteen sea cadet training camps and during the summer 6.SOO sea cadets spent two weeks at camp. The navy provided officers, doctors, instructors, cooks and other personnel to operate the camps and the boys

War Appropriation-Naval Services
had the advantage of some naval training, and the pleasure of swimming, of handling boats and of camp life generally. We hope that in the summer of 1944 some 9,500 sea ,cadets will be able to enjoy the benefit of these camps..
Future prospects. With regard to the future, I may tell the committee that in the coming fiscal year we shall add appreciably to our fleet. This year we hope to acquire from the admiralty two fine modern cruisers and we propose to man two aircraft carriers with naval crews. The acquisition of these larger ships is, I think, desirable from every point of view. They will add to the strength and effectiveness of the Canadian- navy and will give a number of our officers and ratings experience in handling larger ships.
Up to now our navy has been what is commonly called a small-ship navy. Many officers and some ratings have served with the Royal Navy in British ships of the iarger types, but now they will have the opportunity of manning Canadian ships of the larger class.
With regard to the aircraft carriers, I may say that the plan is that the Canadian navy will operate the ships with its own officers and ratings, but the planes and the men to fly them will be provided by the Royal Navy. Besides these larger vessels, cruisers and carriers, we hope to add about 100 other fighting ships as well as a considerable number of auxiliary craft to the strength of the Canadian navy.
In the next year we plan to take in personnel to the number of about 12,000, or at the rate of approximately 1.000 a month.
Post-war. Hitherto, Mr. Chairman, I have talked of the war and its progress. I should like now to say a word about post-war matters.
I listened to the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) last week when he spoke during the discussion of the estimates of the department for air, and I noted his plea, which was in effect that we should get on with the war and spend less time in talk about post-war problems. I have some sympathy, a good deal of sympathy with that view. The supreme task now before this government, and this house and this country is the winning of the war. All other considerations must take second- place to that great consideration, and I am proud to be able to say that, so far as I can gather, that is the view taken by the personnel of the Canadian navy. They are keen, of course, to get. the war against Germany over, and then they feel that they have a few matters to attend to in the Pacific.
They realize that the war is no-t yet won.
IMr. A. L. Macdonald.1
They know that in Europe the enemy is very strong on land, and still strong and dangerous in the air and on the sea. They know that in the Pacific there are long distances to traverse and heavy fighting to be successfully undertaken before the Japanese menace is completely and finally destroyed.
Yet I am unable to agree that we should give no thought now to the welfare of our service men. I do not believe that our successful prosecution of the war will be interfered with by any attention that we might here give to such a matter. Rather do I think that our prosecution of the war will be helped, for this reason; and we all agree that the service man must be well fed and clothed and paid, and must be given periods of leave and recreation, that he must feel that those who are dependent on him shall not suffer want or privation while he is away.
We believe in these things, because they are right and just in themselves and because the service man will be a better service man for our doing them. In a word, we believe in maintaining morale.	.
I am sure that the morale of the service man is improved when he sees the people at home taking an interest in his welfare, and therefore I feel that all civilian groups in this country who try to do something for the service man are discharging a patriotic task.
I believe, for example, that one of the wisest steps we ever took in the naval service was taken when we accepted the suggestion of Captain Brand, one of our own officers, to name corvettes after Canadian cities and towns. That practice has created a link between city or town and the ship, which is helpful to both. Every time that comforts-clothing or cigarettes, books, radios or whatever you will-go from the city to the ship, it proves to the ship's company that the people back home are interested in them, and they are better sailors because of that feeling.
It is inevitable that some service men should be thinking of the post-war world. Should not we here be equally concerned? Should we not try to ensure, so far as we can ensure, that life in this country will be a little better than it was before?	%
I hope that I shall not be misunderstood. I hope I shall not be counted among those who felt that this country before the war was not worth fighting for, that nearly every other land was fairer than this, that other types or systems of government were far superior to ours. No. This country, from the time our fathers first came to it, has been worth fighting for, and, if need be, dying for; and 60,000

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Canadians in the last war, besides many more thousands in this, have proved with their lives the validity of that statement.
Nor do I think for a moment that our service men want fantastic promises and impossible assurances that after the war they will enter upon a new and entirely different sort of life where the state will pour out money in unending and unstinted flow from a magic horn of plenty. What they want most, I suspect, is to take up again the broken skein of their peace-time lives, to return to the families and friends from whom they have been separated, to enjoy once more the privileges and the pleasures and to assume again their share of the responsibilities of Canadian life. What they want is an opportunity to make a decent living at work in this land, at work on the farm, in the factory, in the office, as their fancies and their abilities may dictate. Let us try to give them that opportunity. Let us make to ourselves and to them one pledge, in the words of Lincoln: "To care for him who shall have borne the battle and for his widow and his orphan". Let us do what is right and reasonable for them in the matter of demobilization grants, war service gratuities and pensions. Let us honestly try to help those who need help to reestablish themselves in civil life.
I have no fear that these service men will come back here as wild-eyed revolutionaries. They will have sacrificed much for Canada. They are not likely to tear down the edifice which they risked their lives to defend. Rather, I am certain, will they come back ready to play in peace a role comparable to that which they played in war, defenders and protectors of Canada.
In the naval service, as in the other two services, we have set up a directorate to give study to the problems of demobilization, rehabilitation and kindred matters. We have placed at the head of that directorate a volunteer reserve officer; for this problem is one that is of chief concern to the reserve branches rather than to the permanent forces. He was in the naval reserve before the war and in this war he has had extensive and distinguished sea service. He, and those associated with him, will work with officers from the other services and with officials of other departments such as the Department of Pensions and National Health, and with all the other departments that are interested in the matter.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion that has already taken place in this committee on this problem has been most helpful,
and I hope that members of the committee will continue to give the same earnest and helpful attention that they have already shown. I now leave the estimates of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services to what I know will be the careful, and what I hope will be the kindly, consideration of this committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The committee has listened to the unfolding of a story as told by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services which is based on the wonderful accomplishments of the Canadian people. In the figures which he gave on enlistments he has drawn attention to the most notable point in connection with naval expansion. It has also been drawn to the attention of the world by writers

War Appropriation-Naval Services
from the United States that this far-flung and largely agricultural country of Canada has been responsible for an expansion in naval affairs which the world has certainly never seen before. I remember meeting Commodore Hose in 1934. He was then retiring from the position of chief of the naval staff. He had just returned from a trip across Canada, the purpose of which was to inspect establishments of the naval volunteer reserve. He was most gratified to find wherever he went that those establishments were up to strength, and, peace years though they were, that the training was being carried on which was later to have such notable effect. In that expansion Commodore Hose had a particular part to play, because it was while he was chief of the naval staff that the naval staff produced those plans which have been so efficient in the expansion which the minister was able to describe to-day.
When I left the Department of National Defence the three branches of the naval services included 2,100 officers and ratings, of which but 900 were in the permanent service. By 1939, the smoke having arisen over the European horizon and it having become more and more evident that war was in the offing, that figure, judged by recent departmental papers, had risen to 3,600, and now the minister is able to speak of 80,000. This is a marvellous accomplishment for a country of the size, shape and population of Canada.
But it must not be thought that excellencies alone depend on . numerical expansion. That very expansion, and the rapidity of it, have carried with them verv grave problems of training and the like which had to be solved by. the naval staff, and it is possible that in the further discussion of his estimates the minister will take the committee a little more into his confidence with regard to that work of training. As the ships were required, as the ships were built, ships' complements were necessary. There had to be not only officers commanding; there had to be officers under those officers. In the very early days of new shipbuilding the difficulty was to find officers competent to take on the more specialized duties, for where could the naval staff look for them? They could not look, except in small degree, to the permanent force, which had to take care of the fighting qualities and administrative qualities, as well as to furnish the experience necessary to train men, which experience could be gained only through service. The consequence was that the minister had to turn to the young men who had been taken into the service through the naval volunteer reserve. Courses had to be set up as rapidly as possible and conducted in such
[Mr. Stirling.}
a way that in the shortest possible time the young officers required for these new ships would be forthcoming. But such advances were taking place in the technical end of the naval service that it was necessary to send a certain number of those young specialists to take the courses conducted on the other side of the Atlantic, to take advantage once more of the assistance of the Royal Navy. All through this picture we must remember that we have always had the very great benefit of the assistance of the admiralty and of the Royal Navy.
The Canadian public read with very great interest the references which are continually made in the press to the warlike accomplishments of the Royal Canadian Navy, and well may they do so. I should like also, however, to pay tribute to those others whose services are just as important as those on the fighting ships; for instance, to the wireless operators on our coasts, working away with instruments so novel and so secret that we know nothing about them, but from which information is derived that is absolutely essential in both defensive and offensive work. Then there are those in the convoys. We hear about it when a convoy escort vessel accomplishes some magnificent deed; alas, we hear also when one is lost. From time to time we are told of safe journeys, but I think we should remember that our men are serving day and night, doing valiant service in extreme danger, and that as a result of all this silent work of which we hear so little the valuable tonnage required by the allied nations is safely reaching its destination. Speaking of the convoy escort vessels it is of particular interest, I think-and those who have read the story of the voyage of the Prince oj Wales when she carried the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom to Placenta bay will know to what I refer-that after the Prince of Wales had to cast off her torpedo coverage because of terrible weather, and after she had spent some twenty-four hours with no coverage at all, in the fog of the western Atlantic she was met by a Canadian destroyer which escorted her to Placenta bay. Again, four or five days later, when she left on her return voyage, during the first part of that voyage she was under the protection of Canadian destroyers.
Speaking of the Prince oj Wales, I should like to draw to the committee's attention a remarkable and human incident. On board that ship was a Canadian midshipman, born in Penticton, at the southern end of the Okanagan valley in the riding which I represent. He remained on the Prince of Wales until she was sunk by the Japanese off Singa-

War Appropriation-Naval Services
pore, and he was rescued. Then he went aboard the cruiser Exeter-, subsequently she was sunk, and he was not saved. That occurred on March 13,	1942. No news whatever
reached the parents until a day or two after the New Year, when they received a letter from one who described himself as a member of a small committee that had been endeavouring to ascertain what actually had happened to the Exeter ship's company; and he regretted to say that although they had been able to account for all but six of that company, this lad was one of the six unaccounted for. On January 13 of this year, however, one year and ten months after the Exeter was sunk, the parents received official information that Midshipman Leir had been discovered in a prison camp in Java. This may help to keep alive the hope there must be in the hearts of so many whose loved ones have been reported missing.
As the minister further unfolds his story I hope he will give us more information in regard to what is being done concerning rehabilitation. He has briefly referred to the fact that the matter is under consideration. I wonder how far he can go ini describing to us just what is being done. It is very difficult, yes, impossible, to peer into the future and see with any accuracy what will have to be done; so many factors are still a matter of surmise. I do not suppose, for instance, that the minister can say in so many words even what may be his vision of the Canadian navy after the war. I do not suppose he is able to say how rapidly we shall have to concern ourselves with rehabilitation; but I wonder whether a survey has been conducted among those at present in the navy, to give such information as the number who would like to retire from the service at the end of the war, for example, or whether after the European conflict has subsided the minister foresees the removal of the Royal Canadian Navy to Pacific waters and, as a consequence, the necessity of keeping in commission as many ships as we have in commission to-day.
No doubt if that survey is being conducted the sailors are being asked what they want to do. In that way the minister will be able to supply himself with categorical information which will at least enable him to form his plans for training. In that connection I would ask him whether it is the intention of his department to set up and carry on training classes for sailors only, or whether he intends to lean on the training arrangements conducted under the Department of Pensions and National Health. I should like him to go as far as he can in his answers, because it will be of great assistance to the many people
throughout Canada, who, in groups and as individuals, are turning their attention more and more to problems of reconstruction and rehabilitation. If I understand the position of naval entry aright, with the exception of those candidates, I believe fifty in number, who because of their educational position are able to attain entry into Royal Roads, there is no direct entry into the Royal Canadian Navy.

speechtext: You mean for officers?
