speechtext:
I mean for officers and
men. As I understand1 it, all entry now occurs through the naval volunteer reserve. I am not speaking of those who, because of their experience and service, are able to enter the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, those who have had merchant seaman experience; my understanding is that all entry into the Royal Canadian Navy is via the naval volunteer reserve.
I notice that recruiting advertisements are again appearing in the papers for ordinary seamen, communication ratings and stokers.
Is there a restriction upon recruiting to-day to those listings, or, for instance, may a boy seaman enter? It is evident that the naval volunteer reserve has been successful not only numerically but also by being used solely for entry into the navy. I return once more to the excellent plans which were laid twenty years ago. They have stood the test of time. When the necessity arose at the actual outbreak of war they were capable of that elasticity and expansion which was so necessary. This service has accomplished exactly the need in view.
I do not wish to detain the committee further at this time,.but I trust we shall soon be able to enter upon a discussion of the items as they appear in the schedule.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
pleased to follow the hon. member for Yale ' (Mr. Stirling) who has paid the Royal Canadian Navy such justifiable and high praise. What I have to say this afternoon will be complimentary to the service and I only wish I could say it as nicely as the last speaker.
It would be difficult for me to keep my seat while naval affairs were being discussed because I represent the constituency of Victoria, which includes Esquimalt, the naval base on the Pacific ocean for the Canadian navy.
Esquimalt has had a long and enviable record as far as naval affairs are concerned. Its record in length of years is not as long as that of Quebec or Halifax, but it does go back for a considerable time. It was first used as a naval base by a captain of the Spanish

War Appropriation-Naval Services
navy who sailed1 into the port of Esquimalt in 1790. It was used for the first time by the British navy in 1858, but in 1855 Rear Admiral Bruce, then engaged in the Crimean war, sent a message to Sir James Douglas, then governor of Vancouver island, asking him to prepare buildings at Esquimalt for hospital purposes. Two years later it was occupied by him. Sir James Douglas made such a splendid job of erecting these buildings that two are still in existence.
The harbour of Esquimalt, as is indicated by its name, an Indian name meaning shoaling or gradually sloping shores, provides a safe harbour of some size. It looks out- upon the strait of Juan de Fuca and to the Olympic mountains, some twenty miles away. Its growth since 1858 has been considerable. Today one of the largest dry docks in the British empire and the only dry dock on British soil on the Pacific ocean is located here. I mention these things to show that even in those distant days it had a place in global warfare. We believe it will have a greater place in this war before we are through with our wily enemies in the islands of the Pacific.
This afternoon I wish , to refer principally to the training of men for this navy of ours which has expanded so rapidly from a few small ships to over 700 and from a few hundred men to over 80,000. It was as necessaiy to get experienced and trained officers as it was to get men. As the last speaker has said, there was no place to look for these men except in the civilian population. In 1937 a number of young men in Victoria decided that they would take an active part in Canadian naval affairs in order to be ready should there ever be an occasion when their services would be required. Quite a large number of them went to Naden and started taking these courses at night. Without exception I think * the whole of that original class is now serving as officers with the Canadian navy. Those hon. members who had the privilege of seeing the picture "Action Stations" in room 368 on Tuesday night saw what the Canadian navy does and how they discharge the task that is assigned to them. The No. 1 boy on that particular boat, Ted Simmons, as he is known at Victoria, is a Victoria boy and one of the original class. He was decorated for his part in the action which was shown in that picture, for boarding a German submarine, trying to secure documents from the ship itself when it was sinking, and for being the last man off, and finally to meet our own boats. That same boy at a later date received a bar to his

medal for a similar gallant and brave action in the Mediterranean carried out *with coolness and judgment.
But he is not the only one of those civilian boys who left offices or stores and have since played a gallant part in connection with the navy. A few nights ago I read in a local newspaper that the youngest officer ever to command a cruiser, in either the British or Canadian navy, was a Victoria boy, and he was commanding her at the age of twenty-six. He was another of those boys who left their civilian jobs to do a job of this kind with the navy.
Just about this time in 1940 the department realized that if it were going to have a steady .stream of properly trained and properly selected officers for the navy it must have a place to train them, and with this in mind the department selected what I believe was the best place that could have been found in the Dominion of Canada. They chose what was then known to us on the west coast as Hatley Park, the home of the Hon. James Dunsmuir. It was built at great expense to him, and with great care in the laying out of the property. Without doubt it is the most beautiful spot among the many beautiful spots on Vancouver island. Here is one time when the government secured something at a very low cost. They paid for that property $75,000, which was barely sufficient to pay for the cost of the fence around the property. The property as a whole comprises 640 acres. It faces out on Royal Roads and is close to the Esquimalt naval dockyards and barracks. It has a lagoon, a natural lake, in front, and is a very suitable place for the training of naval personnel. For some years it was used for the purpose of training officers for the navy. I do not know how many of the thousand and more officers from British Columbia now serving in the Canadian navy were actually trained there, but I know there were many men from eastern Canada too who received their training in this school. When the department thought it had trained sufficient officer personnel, it converted this property into what is now the Royal Canadian Naval College. The central building is practically a castle in itself, and there are many outbuildings conforming in architecture and substance to the central building. In addition, the government has built a training school, which also does credit to the architect who designed it and to (he navy itself.
I want to give a word of explanation for the benefit of many hon. members who, I hope, will take occasion to visit this college before

War Appropriation-Naval Services
long. I took a minister out to see that property, and after he had seen it he said as we were coming back over the winding road through the bush, which is beautiful, "What luxury!" Well, they are luxurious quarters, and an endeavour was made to take some of the trimmings away so that the place would not look quite so luscious. The whole place was carpeted with a red carpet like may be seen in the other chamber. There was an elaborate billiard room, containing one of the finest billiard tables I think I have ever seen, and gorgeous crystal chandeliers. At the time the negotiations were going on I suggested to the man who was negotiating the deal that we should not purchase these appurtenances because it might be misunderstood by the taxpayers who might visit that piece of property. My advice was accepted, but it did not work out just the way he had thought it would, because other people became interested in this college and in the site and donated the elaborate chandeliers and the rich red carpet. The late Sir Edward Beatty thought the billiard table was a proper thing to have at the college and accordingly he donated it to the school. I make this explanation to remove any impression there might be that the government was spending the people's money unnecessarily.
I maintain that any boy who attends the naval college in Victoria enjoys a rare privilege. There are some twenty-one officers in the school, and they are selected with care. Hon. members would be delighted to meet and to know any one of them. The boys who go there are carefully selected, and mostly by quota, from all the provinces. None of them is under fifteen years and eight months and none is over seventeen years and eight months; all are. physically fit, all splendid looking boys. Physical fitness and ability to make full use of their time are the principal qualifications. I have made it a practice to go out there, and my visits are indeed an inspiration to me. I am sorry that we graduate only fifty boys a year from that school, because it is the symbol of the future of our Canadian navy. We must see to it that we shall never again be in the same position as we were in during the fall of 1939. As I understand it, not all the boys are obliged to join the Canadian navy, but all are obliged to be a reserve for the Canadian navy should they be called upon. I believe that when the time comes they will give a good account of their stewardship and show themselves worthy of their training.
I do not wish to take up much time, but I have three or four suggestions to leave with
the minister which I believe, if adopted, would considerably strengthen our position on the Pacific coast so far as the navy is concerned. It was thought some time ago, and I am not finding fault with the conclusion, that it would be advisable to have the senior officers of the three services located on the mainland and together. Now, with the turn of affairs in the Pacific, would be the right time to have the commanding officer of the navy on the Pacific coast and his staff go back to Esquimalt, where they would be at the very heart of naval affairs, rather than remain on the mainland.
My second suggestion is that because of weather conditions-and certainly there is no better climate in Canada-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
-than the climate on the southern end of Vancouver island-north Vancouver may come next-at least preliminary and elementary training of the boys should as far as possible be carried out at Esquimalt. We on the west coast appreciate the fact that the major activity for the Canadian navy is on the Atlantic coast. We hope that will change, and change soon. Until it does we know that the finishing off of our boys can be better done where there is more equipment with which to do it. But during the first stages of their training they can work more days out of doors and be comfortable on the southern end of the island, at Esquimalt, than they can at any other place.
Another suggestion I would make to the minister is that, to round out the training for Vancouver island and for British Columbia generally, a training ship should be stationed at Esquimalt, not only to train naval personnel but to train men for the merchant marine service as well.
It may be remembered that when I was giving a short history of Esquimalt I said that the first occupation of that harbour was for hospital purposes. At that time it was not thought it was too far to bring wounded soldiers from the Black sea, where they were then fighting, to Esquimalt. I think that to-day Canada should supply hospital accommodation not merely for her own personnel but for the personnel of any of our allies, or even our enemies, who might have to come to British Columbia. I know plans are going forward for further hospital accommodation, and it takes some time. We are not impatient about that; we are glad that they are proceeding as quickly as possible. But I press again, and I think I am right in doing so, that we should look further than merely to

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the care of our own personnel as far as hospitalization is concerned at that particular point.
Another matter to which I should like to call the minister's attention is the lack of the best kind of equipment for the speedy repairing of ships at Esquimalt harbour. I think we should be in a position to take care quickly and adequately of any ship, no matter what its size, which may become disabled in the Pacific and the tools for that purpose should be provided. Probably some of them are so large that they would be used only once or twice in the next twenty-five years or longer, but the quick repairing of a ship when it may come to our coast at this time is one of the protections which we should provide.
I have only one further remark to make. This is the first occasion on which I have spoken in the chamber this year, and I do not. expect to speak very often. I have noticed here, during this session and the last, criticism of various departments which might well have been made, and better made, in other ways. As long as we are a democracy -and I am quite sure we shall always enjoy that form of government-the minister in submitting his estimates must not only give a balance sheet but submit as well in most instances the history of each item connected therewith. I am not one to say that we should not criticize, but in war time our criticism should be reduced to the minimum, and in fact it should be so sparing that, if it were a time of peace, it might be called slackness. On many occasions, however, criticism has a tendency to make the people of Canada waiver in their estimate of the way in which the war is going. For my part, on every occasion, in my own feeble way I have tried to impress upon my people at home that the first duty of every Canadian is to stand steadfast during the war. We should not be carried away with success, nor should we be unduly depressed by losses. We must be prepared to stand steady and to carry on with our job, and anything that disturbs the people of Canada in that regard is detrimental. It is deterrent to our war effort.
I suggest that many of the things We are talking about to-day in this House of Commons will look very small indeed and entirely out of place when they are stacked up against what may happen to us when the second front opens up and our casualties begin to come back. We shall not then be worrying about this allowance and that allowance; we shall be wishing that we could call up the

fellows lost on those beaches so that they might receive any allowance whatever. I think we should try to keep that in mind.
I do not believe the Canadian people will ever elect a parliament that will not recognize its full obligation to the boys who have fought and those who have died for us. I think we can safely leave to any government that may come into power the responsibility of adequately looking after the rehabilitation of these men, believing that they will not do so in any niggardly, half-hearted or penny-pinching manner, but will fully recognize the obligation of those of us who are enjoying at the present time the protection which these men afford us.

[DOT] But the present minister had an opportunity that none of his predecessors had, and I am pleased to say that he has lived up to the best expectations we all formed of his ability to carry outTiis responsibility. Kitchener and

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had just paid a very short but well-deserved tribute to the late Sam Harris, former president of the Navy League of Canada. When Mr. Harris became president of the league, following the last war, he had a most difficult task to keep alive any sentiment or interest in naval affairs, but. he did his job well. I might also have said a word about the late Aemilius Jarvis, who I believe was the founder of the Navy League of Canada ; I joined it about the same time, but I know the late Mr. Jarvis was ahead of us all. To-day we have as head of the Navy League a gentleman who I am sure is well known to the minister, Mr. David Gibson. It is greatly to the credit of Canada that a man like Mr. Gibson, a big business executive, should be willing to devote so much time and energy to assist the department, through the Navy League, in building up the personnel of the Canadian navy. For some years now we have also had as the capable and brilliant secretary of the Ontario division of the league, Mr. Frank Trimble, who during the last war did a man's job with the Y.M.C.A. and is now doing a man's job in assisting the minister and the department to develop and maintain a naval sentiment throughout the country.
I was interested in what the minister said about the shipyards and the men working in them. I should like to add my tribute, and I might say also that I am happy to know that the technical schools throughout the country have made such a contribution in this regard. Perhaps I might refer in particular to the large technical school in Toronto, where they have shops for the training of engineers and mechanics of every description, the graduates of which have done a fine job in helping build these ships. The minister said something about the marine railways; I suppose he was referring to the shipyards.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: To the naval yards partly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

I was just going to say that perhaps from experience gained through the use of these marine railways in naval yards something may result when the war is over in connection with the building of a marine railway across the Chignecto isthmus in the minister's own province, between the bay of Fundy and Northumberland strait. I think the time is long past when something should be done to save the thousand miles of travel that would be saved by the construction of such a marine railway.
Earlier in the discussion the hon. member for Spadina asked a question about the Toronto naval barracks. This question was asked previously by the hon. member for Broadview, and I might add that all the Toronto members received letters similar to that received by the hon. member for Broadview. I remember some years ago, when the Ontario division of the Navy League built its own headquarters out on the lake shore road west of the exhibition grounds. At that time we hoped that a naval barracks would be built in the same vicinity, but apparently that is not to be so. I am heartily in accord with the erection of a naval barracks in Toronto; I think the city and the province deserve it, and I am glad the minister has taken an interest in the matter. I think the property now being considered is east of the exhibition grounds, and that is a first-class site; it will, I understand, be close to York barracks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

I am looking forward to the time when the minister will see his way clear to bring in an item to cover the construction of this naval barracks in Toronto.
Some time ago I asked about the training of young Canadians to fly from aircraft carriers, and no doubt the minister will have some announcement to make in that regard. I know that a number of young men from. Toronto and other parts of Ontario enlisted and were dispatched overseas, apparently under the direction of overseas authorities, to receive this kind of training. I am not finding fault with that at all; they have to train somewhere, and perhaps these young lads wanted to fly from carriers. However, I am looking forward to the minister's report in that connection; and later on, if the war lasts long enough and Canada has aircraft carriers of its own, perhaps these young Ontario lads may be brought back and given an opportunity of flying from Can-

War Appropriation-Naval Services
ada's own carriers. I do not at all discount the wonderful work that has been done by the old country people; perhaps I should not even suggest that our own boys should come back, but if Canada is to have aircraft carriers then I think it would be only right that young lads from Canada should be brought back to fly from them.
I wish to thank whoever it was that corrected me earlier as to the number from Ontario who had enlisted in the navy. The minister stated the figures correctly, but apparently I jotted1 them down wrong. I had the figure as around eight or nine thousand, but during the dinner hour I reviewed the figures in the Hansard office and I find that the number is well on to 30,000 ratings and something over
2,000	officers. Well, as an Ontario man I am proud to see the wonderful part my native province has played in providing personnel for the naval ships of this country. In conclusion,
I thank the minister and congratulate him upon the good job he is doing.
Mr. MeCUAIG:	I am glad to have the
opportunity of following my good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), because I know he always takes a keen interest in the work of this house and particularly in anything having to do with construction, such as shipbuilding and so on.
As I listened to the minister eloquently telling the wonderful story of our navy this afternoon, I could not help but wish that the people of Canada might have had an opportunity to be present and hear that story as it was told to us. We all realize that in the last number of years, particularly at the beginning of the war, the people of Canada became air-minded. We were able to see the planes overhead and we could see the airfields located throughout the dominion. However, the difficulty with the navy is that it is to be found only on the east and west coasts. We who live in the central parts of Canada do not have the opportunity of familiarizing ourselves with its work.
The minister referred this afternoon to the
difficulties which had been encountered in connection with shipbuilding, and I should like to confine my remarks mainly to that reference. In my own constituency at Col-lingwood we have a shipyard which has done great work in connection with the building of ships during this war. The minister mentioned that at the beginning of the war there were practically no shipyards building ships in Canada. We were probably fortunate in the fact that the shipyard at Collingwood had built some mine-sweepers and other vessels in the few years preceding the war, but when
they were given orders after the war began they had considerable difficulty in getting experienced men. Many of the men whom they had had some twenty or thirty years ago had gone into other occupations and although they could get men to work, they were unable to get the key men essential for shipbuilding.
They could have gone out and got men elsewhere, but that would have meant taking them away from other essential work. Therefore they adopted a plan, which I think was a good one, of training their own men to handle these key positions. That probably slowed down their operations during the first few months of the war, but I think their work has benefited on account of the plan they followed. When we once more have peace I hope the people will not say, "Let us have no more ships; let us discard our shipyards." If those suggestions are carried out and the time ever comes again when we need ships we shall be in the same position we were in four years ago. I suggest to those who will be in charge when peace comes again, to see to it that shipbuilding is continued, not only to ensure a supply of ships but also to keep available those key men who are essential for the manufacture of ships.
I was glad when the decision was made to build some of the smaller ships such as corvettes and mine-sweepers because these could be built in plants on the great lakes. When they are completed they can be taken down through the great lakes, the St. Lawrence river and through to the sea. It has been found that the work performed by these corvettes has added greatly to the protection we have received on the seas. Their principal work is in connection with convoys from Canada to Great Britain. It may only be a coincidence, but it is interesting to note that as the corvettes began to come into operation, which was early in 1941, ship losses immediately declined. Early in the summer of 1941 quite a number of corvettes were put into operation, and on September 30, 1941, Prime Minister Churchill said in the British House of Commons that ship losses from enemy action for July, August and September of that year were only one-third of what they had been in the three preceding months. As I say, that may be only a coincidence, but that is what happened.
The first corvette put into operation after the commencement of the war was H.M.C.9. Collingwood, built in the Collingwood shipyards. Two other corvettes built in those yards were also named after towns in my county, Orillia and Barrie. The keel for the Collingwood was laid in February, 1940; the ship was christened in July, 1940, and she was

War Appropriation-Naval Services
commissioned and delivered in November, 1940. The keel for the Orillia was laid in the month of March, 1940; the ship was christened in September, 1940, and she was commissioned and delivered in November, 1940. These ships were started early in 1940, and at least two went out before the end of the year from the Collingwood shipyard.
I was interested in hearing the minister state this afternoon that the plan of naming ships after towns and cities had been adopted following a suggestion by Captain Brand. The corvette Barrie was christened by Mrs. Brand, who afterwards took a great deal of interest in the ship and provided assistance to the women of different organizations in that municipality which worked to supply woollens, radios and other equipment for the comfort of the sailors. We were perhaps also fortunate in having as the commander of that ship Lieutenant-Commander Roy M. Mosher. He was born in Nova Scotia and has often been described as a rough diamond but a loyal and capable officer. He endeared himself to the women of our town, and after he left he continued to write letters to the different organization which had been supplying the comforts. I remember reading one letter which was passed over to me in which he said that after he left Collingwood he went to the east coast where his wife was living and arrived there just in time to become the proud father of a son or, as he said, "just in time for the launching". What pleased us more than anything was the fact that he and Mrs. Mosher agreed to calling the boy "Barrie".
I mention these things to show how the different municipalities become interested in the navy, and, it may be, also in the air force. This interest is enhanced by the kindly expressions of people like Captain and Mrs. Brand, and Lieutenant-Commander Mosher.

Mr. Chairman, before I discuss the estimates of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), I should like to refer briefly to another naval matter. Last Monday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) put on the record of this house the names of two gallant Canadians who had been awarded the Victoria Cross, Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt of Vancouver and Captain P. Triquet of Cabano, Quebec. A little later on the leader of the opposition put on the record the name of Private William Manley who had won the Victoria Cross in Libya while serving in the British army. He felt as I do that any Canadian fighting in the British forces or in the Canadian forces is fighting for his country and deserving of honour in this house. With 
that in mind I should like to adorn the record of this house with the name of a fourth Canadian who has won the Victoria Cross, Captain P. T. Peters of the Royal Navy. Captain Peters was born in Prince Edward Island but early showed his good judgment and wisdom by moving to British Columbia-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Question!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: -where he settled down in the city of Nelson. I may add that he is undoubtedly the most decorated Canadian in this war, having made a clean sweep of decorations for gallantry in the face of the enemy, because he has also won the D.S.O. and the D.S.C.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Royal Navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should like to congratulate the minister upon his presentation of the exploits of the Royal Canadian Navy. I am sure that every Canadian is very proud of both the expansion of the navy and the job which has been done by our navy fighting in its little ships in the north Atlantic. It is a pity perhaps that this house has not among its members a naval officer or rating to bring a whiff of the salt sea air into this chamber. On the other hand, the navy is known as the silent service, and he might feel out of place in the House of Commons as a silent member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: He would have plenty of company.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
And a colleague behind me suggests that he would be all right as an Ontario member. I do not pretend in this house to be the spokesman of soldiers, sailors or airmen, but I think this is one time I can speak on behalf of every soldier, sailor and airman overseas when I tell the committee of the admiration they all hold for the work done by the Royal Canadian Navy. After all, their first contact with operations is when they go in convoy across the north Atlantic to the old country. I think most of us find it a pretty shaking experience, and when we set foot in England we heave a great sigh of relief and suddenly we realize that the navy has to do that job again and again until the end of the war.
The minister mentioned the part the Canadian navy played in the war in the Mediterranean. I think that when the whole story of the war in Africa and the Mediterranean is written it will not be the eighth army or the desert air force that will get the greatest measure of credit and honour, but the Royal

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Navy under Sir Andrew Cunningham. Very briefly I should like to remind the committee, because it is a story that is not well known, of the part they played. There would not have been a man, a plane, a gun, not even a tin of bully beef in Libya but for_the grace of the British navy. Every man, every tank and every plane came the long way around from England, around the Cape of Good Hope and up the Red Sea into Egypt. It was the Royal Navy that strangled Rommel, that cut off his petrol and ammunition supplies in the Mediterranean, and that made the victory at El Alamein possible. It was the Royal Navy which hurled the heaviest artillery into the ports of North Africa, which were so great a factor in that war. It was the Royal Navy which took that enormous armada of 3,200 ships of every size and shape safely across the waters on the invasion of Sicily, and I think its greatest day or night was September 14 at Salerno, when the beachhead threatened to turn into another Dunkirk. The British navy steamed in close to shore and threw a solid barrage of steel, everything they had, from their 16-inch guns down to their smallest guns, and we held the beachhead. Now they are doing it again at Anzio, and with great loss, as we read in the papers.
I think in every Briton's heart there beats tremendous pride in the British navy, whether it be in our blood, or whether it be our traditions or the songs and stories that we learned in our youth. Certainly, the most memorable sight that I saw in this war was the navy. The good book, of course, speaks of an army with banners. Its modern equivalent would perhaps be tanks going into battle, and certainly a squadron of aircraft taking off for Germany is a moving sight. But nothing is quite so stirring to a Briton as a British man-of-war putting out to sea.
I remember the night we embarked from the grand harbour at Malta for the invasion of Sicily. It was last July. We had been there a month while the squadrons were doing the bombing and softening up of Sicily before the great day of the invasion came. It was a warm July evening when we went down to the Grand harbour at Malta and loaded on a landing barge on a little beach just under the towering cliffs of Valetta. Once aboard we were all tense. I remember well the palms of my hands were a little wet and my lips a little dry, and there was a loose feeling in my bowels perhaps-not that we were afraid, but it is something like starting an election campaign. You know you can do it but you are waiting for it to get under way. Then
down the harbour came a great sight-the Rodney, the Nelson and the Indomitable putting out to sea, and after them cruisers, destroyers, torpedo boats, and a great fleet of invasion barges. The British navy is great for show and tradition, even when going into battle, for as they sailed down the harbour they dressed ship as a salute to heroic Malta. The blue-jackets in their tropical whites stood side by side along the bows of the Rodney and the Nelson, with the Royal Marines in khaki drill with white topees and white piped webbing lined up around the stern, and on the great flight deck of the aircraft carrier Indomitable the brass band played "Hearts of Oak". The airmen on our barge looked [DOT] at the sight and said, "Thank God we have the navy."
It was that sight which determined me when I returned to Canada to come back by a ship of the Royal Canadian Navy. So that when I arrived in London last fall I went to Canadian headquarters. Even there I found a pleasant thing. Overseas our army and our air force had felt that Canada should put on a good show and they have palatial headquarters. But the navy does things in a very modest way. Half of one floor of a very small office building, and not in one of the best parts of London, is where the Royal Canadian Navy carries on its overseas headquarters.
I was given every courtesy, and I can tell this committee that half an hour after I entered I left all booked up, time and place and port, to return to Canada. The service could not have been excelled by any steamship line in civilian life, and I wish to thank the minister now for the courtesy extended to me over there. I should like to tell the committee just a little bit, from a landlubber's point of view, of life with the Canadian navy at sea. I embarked at the port of Londonderry -I do not think that is giving away any secret -and expecting the voyage to be rough and cold, I wore an old suit of battledress. I was rather ashamed when I got on deck to see everybody else looking spic and span in their tiddly blue, the officers in gleaming gold braid, and the sailors so natty with their little hats tipped over one eye, I thought I was letting the air force down by wearing my old suit of battledress. Therefore the following morning I came up in my very best blues, looking very swish, I thought, and I discovered I had made a mistake again because, once at sea, I found the sailors of the Canadian navy were just as Canadians at a hockey rink. They were wearing sweaters, ski jackets and balaclava helmets, any kind of worn dress for convenience and comfort. They were now Canadians at sea, fighting.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The actual forming of the convoy was a wonderful sight. The great ships formed up, the destroyers and corvettes and the whole flotilla under the commodore. I wish to pay a tribute to these commodores, who I think are the most heroic figures in this war. They are old British admirals long since retired from their fighting ships, but when the war came they left their firesides and went back to sea, some of them' seventy, some seventy-five, and one I know, eighty years of age, with faces the colour of port, and hearts-I cannot describe their hearts. These are the men who have led the convoys back and forth across the Atlantic.
We had thought that we in Libya were ' living under rather desperate conditions. Mind you, since I have got back and started . talking about it the conditions have become more and more desperate; at times I am rather surprised to find that I have survived. But I can tell this committee that the Canadian navy, fighting in these little ships, lives under conditions very much more exacting than the life out in Libya. By their very nature these little ships have not very much in the way of accommodation. A destroyer is away nearly all the time. These old British destroyers and the United States destroyers we have are very poorly heated, if they are heated at all. But these men in the Canadian ships, the destroyers and fair-miles and corvettes and mine-sweepers, live , and fight under these conditions: they have,
I think, perhaps the. finest spirit of any of our fighting services. There is a healthy rivalry between the ships. The Kootenay for example thinks it is the best ship in the fleet; that the Skeena, the Saguenay, the Saskatchewan and the rest of them are not in their class. It is a very fine thing for a man to believe so thoroughly that his own ship is the finest ship afloat.
There is another circumstance, of course, which binds the men of the navy so close together. In the army and the air force, for every combatant in the front line, there are ten, fifteen or twenty non-combatants in various distances behind. In the navy, every man on a destroyer or a corvette, from the skipper on the bridge to the stoker in the hold and the cooks and stewards in the galley, are taking exactly the same risks; they experience, the same hazards; they have the same pride in their ship. The convoy on which I sailed was the first convoy back after the launching of the acoustic torpedo which had resulted in the sinking of the St. Croix. In this country we are inclined to think that the Royal Navy, the British navy, is slow and tradition-bound. To me it was amazing that,

in the seven or eight days which elapsed between the arrival of that convoy and the sailing of ours, the British navy had devised the answer to the acoustic torpedo. The men in the navy were frightfully keen, like fishermen going out with a new lure, to try out this new gear. When action stations rang the fourth night out it was amazing to see the ship transformed; all the men from cooks and stokers upwards knew where they were going and where they had to fight, and manned their posts with the most incredible enthusiasm. This was their chance to see if their gear would work and to get "one up" on the other destroyers of the Canadian navy.
As far as living conditions are concerned, a very great deal has been done for the Canadian navy both by the towns which have adopted these ships and by the Navy League and the women's organizations across this countiy. If there is one thing these men at sea need it is warm clothing, and they have received it in substantial quantities, but the quantity must be increased from all parts of Canada.
I should like to speak briefly now on the navy as it affects the Pacific coast. I am the member representing half of Vancouver harbour, which is the biggest year-round harbour in Canada. On the United States side are four great Pacific coast harbours-San Diego, San Pedro for Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Seattle-each one of them having a big naval establishment. The great city of Vancouver, however, has not a single naval dock or pier. There is one small barracks at Dead Man's island. The reason is obvious. We had an old and established naval base, of which the hon. member for Victoria spoke so well this afternoon, Esquimalt, established by the British government in 1853. When the British government established Esquimalt the mainland of British Columbia was pretty well a howling wilderness. Vancouver harbour was used only by the Indians. All naval supplies came by sea into Esquimalt, so the fact that Esquimalt was on an island was no handicap. Now, however, this situation has changed. All supplies or almost all supplies for Esquimalt come from the mainland of Canada; they pass through the harbour of Vancouver, and over civilian docks and by civilian transport to Esquimalt. The time has surely come when Vancouver should have naval docks and naval piers, so that naval supplies transferred between Vancouver and Esquimalt can be handled with purely service facilities. Vancouver is well equipped for this purpose, because we have plenty of good land, and deep sea anchorage; that is, in North Vancouver, and

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the two biggest and best shipyards in Canada.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has shown great interest in what part the army and air force are to be permitted to play in the war against Japan. If there is one service which will play a very important part, we know it to be our navy, and when our navy moves to the west coast, Vancouver and Esquimalt must be its principal bases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: And Prince Rupert.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will include the great seaport of the hon. member for Skeena. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that the time has come to build and plan on the west coast for the winding up by our navy of the war against Japan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) praise the boys of the navy. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. McCuaig) mentioned shipbuilding, but it is the men of the navy, the men who man the ships, who are the real heroes.
Corvettes have been mentioned. I do not believe reference has been made to the Fairmiles and the mine-sweepers. I know, from boys who have been on these ships in convoy work and patrolling, and in these minesweepers, that sometimes for days on end they have to stand up to their meals; the meals, just as they are, perhaps uncooked, are passed to them, because the corvettes and minesweepers and Fairmiles do not merely pitch; they roll and toss. It takes an extremely strong man to stand up under these conditions, and these boys and men deserve every bit of credit the Canadian people can give them; they have done a wonderful job and are continuing to do it.
Just here I wish to read a short article which was in the newspaper on March 2. It is entitled, "Six Tiny Fairmiles Ride Gale; Guard Convoy Through Night", and states:
Six tiny Fairmile launches pushed their sleek noses into the teeth of the worst maritime blizzard in years. February 24, on sudden orders to supply patrol protection, presumably for a
convoy.
The story of the 12-hour, night-long battle of the little ships and their crews, withheld until now for security reasons, was disclosed to-day by naval headquarters. Details of their job were not given. It was merely disclosed they performed duty normally expected of "big ships".
Manned chiefly by volunteer reserve men, the patrol craft suffered no damage despite high seas, lashing snow and spray driven by a 50-mile-an-hour wind. Visability was cut to 200 yards. The period was an anxious one for even the largest ships in the area.
The performance of the motor-launches in a storm which saw many marine accidents and
ships driven ashore drew the first signal of praise in this war for that type of work. Rear Admiral L. W. Murray, commander in chief, Canadian Northwest Atlantic, signalled commendations to the ships, which operate under Captain J. A. Heenan of Ottawa.
When I was in Halifax, Admiral Murray suggested that if I ever got the chance I should see the motion picture entitled, "Corvete K225". If any hon. member here has not seen that picture he certainly should see it. It gives one an idea of what these boys have to go through and what they are doing.
I am very much interested in the navy owing to the fact that the Grove school is in my riding. There are over 260 old boys on its honour roll. These boys have joined the navy, and I may say that Vice-Admiral Nelles went to school at Grove, as did many of the officers of the Canadian and Royal navies. I believe it was the first institution in Canada to have a sea cadet corps, and I know that during 1940, 1941 and 1942 the flag at the school was at half-mast practically all the time for boys who had gone to the school.and had afterwards lost their lives fighting in the Canadian navy. During 1943 there were not as. many sinkings, and therefore the flag was not quite so often at half-mast.
The reason why Grove school is perhaps the first to have established a sea cadet corps in Canada is, in my opinion, the fact that Peterborough, the riding I have the honour to represent, is one of the boating paradises of Canada.
The minister to-day did not mention the officers of the Canadian Pacific Steamships' personnel. I find in the press of March 6 an article with reference to Canadian Pacific Steamships' officers who have been honoured. I quote:
As part of the 5,599 Canadian Pacific Steamships' personnel on admiralty, armed cruiser and shore service, ten officers have been honoured by the king "for good services" in vessels from among the twenty Canadian Pacific ships taken over by the admiralty in 1939. Awards for heroism won by the Canadian Pacific seagoing personnel in this war now total forty-one. The newcomers to join the honour roll are:
Captain R. A. Leicester, O.B.E., master of a vessel sunk in the Mediterranean when Engineer Officers Edward E. Stewart and William B. Harris, both of Victoria, won M.B.E.'s.
Chief Officer Donald Smith, O.B.E., of Vancouver and First Officer Leonard Johnston, M.B.E., of Vancouver, who guided refugees to safety after the Japs sunk their ship, the Empress of Asia, off Singapore.
Chief Engineer William JVeilson, O.B.E., of Victoria and Captain L. C. Barry, M.B.E., for more than two years continuous operation "in dangerous waters".

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Captain George Goold and Chief Officer John St. Claire Clarke, both of Vancouver, and Chief Engineer D. Cowper commended for their actions when the Italians sunk the Empress of Canada off West Africa.
The minister did not say anything to-day as to whether Canada intended to build any aeroplane carriers for our navy. I think he should have let the committee know what is going to be done along that line, because the Canadian navy will have to carry planes perhaps before this war is over and certainly before another war comes along.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
One cannot help being greatly impressed with the account the minister has given of the activities of the navy. Its growth from a small pre-war permanent force of 1,700 personnel to over 74,000 is a record of which any country may be proud. Indeed, I understand that the personnel of our navy is now greater in extent than that of the Royal Navy in peace time. In addition to that number of 74,000, we must not overlook the establishment of the Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service, which has grown since the autumn of 1942, when the first class was started, to a personnel of over 4,500, and to the Wrens I should like to pay a special tribute.
Our Canadian boys have proven themselves great sailors; and it has amazed all how the young lads, not only from the maritime provinces but from one end of the country to the other, including the prairies, have taken to the sea as if it were their native haunt. So high is the tradition of the British navy, so strong is the lure of the sea, that when a poll was taken at a boys' school near Toronto to ascertain which of the three services was the most popular the navy won the vote.
It is not my 'intention to praise the minister for naval services any more than I would praise the minister for air, whose partisanship when in opposition was notorious. I am not in a position to know how much better their tasks might have been fulfilled, but there are so many stout fellows in the navy as well as in the other services that I feel we cannot pay too great a tribute to their ability and to their eagerness to serve where the danger is greatest. At the same time, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) has not hesitated to adopt new ideas or, if I read correctly between the lines, to make changes in personnel in a quiet way for the betterment of the great service which is the particular care of his department.
The heroism of the men in the silent service will go down in the annals of our country. I think of one of my young friends who, in the early days of the war, lost his life when in command of the leading motor-torpedo boat tMr. G. H. Fraser.)
in a raid which blocked the harbour of St. Nazaire. I recall another young man from my own riding who was on a corvette that rammed a submarine off the coast of Cuba, a youth who entered the navy as a rating on leaving school, and whose ability has now been recognized by his promotion to a sublieutenancy.
Our part m conquering the submarine menace has been a notable contribution to the war effort, for as long as that menace persisted there was little chance of organizing an effective invasion of the nazi fortress of Europe. Great Britain, in appreciation of our contribution to the common cause and of our ability to man and sail ships of war, has given Canada, by way of reverse mutual aid, two cruisers which will constitute the nucleus of capital ships for the Royal Canadian Navy.
May I add a word to the praise which the minister has already given to those splendid young women who are members of the W.R.C.N.S. The Wrens have so proved their effectiveness as an integral part of the navy in Great Britain that it was decided that the formation of a like organization in Canada would be a needed and desirable contribution to the war effort on the part of our country, relieving, as it does in some degree, our manpower shortage. At our request we borrowed from the Women's Royal Naval Service of Great Britain three of their officers to assist in setting up the W.R.C.N.S. in Canada. In April, 1942, Superintendent Carpenter, notwithstanding failing health at that time, cheerfully and ably carried out the task to which she had been assigned. After resuming duties in Great Britain she was awarded the order of Commander of the British Empire. Accompanying her was Captain Isherwood, who remained for a somewhat longer time in Canada as the first head of the W.R.C.N.S.
The high standards of the Canadian Wrens owe much to the organizing and administrative ability of Superintendent Carpenter and Captain Isherwood. Accompanying these two officers was Lieutenant Sturdee, a granddaughter of the famous admiral of that name who fought at the battle of Jutland.
While selective recruiting for Wrens was still going on apace, the present Director of Wrens, Commander Sinclair, was assigned to the British Wrens, and on the return of Captain Isherwood to Great Britain, Commander Sinclair took over the command and has since that time devoted to the organization her high executive talents.
May I here pay a tribute to Great Britain for her contribution in helping in organizing the Canadian Wrens, as well as in offering the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
model for the Canadian navy. I do this not because the contribution comes from across the water but because that contribution represents the highest development which the experience of centuries has given to a service that stands ever ready and ever eager to serve its country. To appreciate fully the contribution which the Wrens are making to our war effort it is necessary to review their activities which have in virtually all cases been the means of releasing sailors for active service'. They have replaced men in map plotting, signalling, as dietitians, cooks, waiters, sick-berth attendants, drivers, clerks, typists, and in the handling of mail, messengers, et cetera. May I read an extract from the official pamphlet "Canada at War" for January of this year:
A Wren officer is captain of a training ship ashore-first woman to achieve that distinction; another officer graduated from an accounting officers' course with male officers; a Wren is doing medical research for the navy in a guarded laboratory; Wren dietetics officers (under Lieut.-Commander Taylor) supervise the food eaten by naval personnel ashore or afloat; a Wren officer instructs seamen cooks at the naval cooking school at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis at Deep Brook, N.S.; a Wren checked all the shipping through the Welland canal during the navigation season.
As the minister mentioned, the Wrens are serving at over thirty different naval bases in Canada, Washington, Newfoundland and overseas. Indeed, one British guest child who came to Canada in the early days of the war has since returned and is now a stoker Wren running a harbour craft in one of the British ports. That she is a granddaughter of the Lord Chancellor of Great Britain is only an indication of the high quality of the young women who seek service in the Wrens. No less worthy of mention is the fact that the daughter of my office mate, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) is a driver Wren.
Owing to the high type of young woman who has been attracted to the senior service, there has been little occasion for disciplinary action. The excellent training which the Wrens are receiving and the fact that they are serving together in an organization with the highest ideals of service, are making them not only better women, but better citizens of our great country.

speechtext:
Along with other hon. members I have listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's presentation. I was particularly interested1 in his winding-up remarks. I think the minister was perhaps more realistic at that point than during all the rest of his address, because most of his address con-100-S4
sisted of putting statistics on the record, showing the growth and development of the navy. I am sure we all join with him in that connection in expressing our appreciation of a job well done. However, the minister stated and reiterated what the ministers of national defence for army and air stated, that our first and most important obligation is the winning of the war and that we must not lose sight of the fact that it is far from won. Second, the minister sharply disagreed with some hon. members on this side of the house, and I think rightly so, in their criticism of spending any time of the committee on post-war problems. I believe the minister was absolutely right when he stated1 that in order to build up the morale of those in the fighting services- all three of them-it was necessary that we at home demonstrate-particularly those in the House of Commons-from time to time that we are not unmindful of the fact that they are fighting not only against something but for something; that we in this House of Commons know what they are fighting for, and that we are utilizing our time to lay down a programme and policy with respect to the organization of the economic resources of the country to guarantee to them, as the minister stated, that when they come back they will return to a Canada that will assure them of equality of opportunity, the right to a job, and the right to earn a living. As we discuss the problems that come before the house from time to time I do not think we must lose sight of that for a moment. I believe that any time used in this house in discussions with respect to post-war problems is time well spent. I believe it is one of the most important things that this committee can do, particularly if we have those in the services in mind and if we desire to send them forward to make their greatest contribution. That contribution can only be made when they realize that we back here are doing something to change the scheme of things from what it was when war broke out. That is the greatest morale builder that we in Canada can undertake for those in the services.
So far in the debate members from both parties in the committee have risen and have led the minister to believe that his job is completed, or at least there has been no criticism. The speeches so far have consisted of straight eulogies of the presentation. Some hon. members have been doing a little job here and there for their own constituencies. As I see it, the function of the opposition is to accept what the government has to offer and to criticize any proposal that comes before the committee-constructively, of course-in order to urge the government forward to a greater



War Appropriation-Naval Services
effort. I believe that can best be done by taking the policy that existed in the past year, boiling it down to cases and pointing out for the benefit of the minister just where that policy did not live up to expectation.
From time to time ministers rise in their places in the committee and say: "Individual cases should not be discussed in the committee". There is no other practical way possible that I know of whereby improvements can be made than by mention of individual cases. That is the most specific and shortest way of demonstrating to a minister the ineffectiveness of his programme as it is being administered in the country. The best way to do it is to boil it down and exemplify it. That is the shortest, most concrete and most specific way in which it can be done. I disagree with those who say that individual cases should not be discussed in the committee. A very good policy can be ruined by faulty administration, and any minister of government, particularly a minister of a war department, who has a large organization that extends in many directions is certainly not in a position to keep his finger on every specific detail of administration as it affects the people of the country. Some official or officials perhaps not as familiar with regulations as they should be, can create a situation in the country, unknown to the minister, that is adverse to the whole policy of the department. The shortest and most specific way of bringing that to his attention is to give him the case, because in my opinion a case arises in either one of two- ways, either through an inefficient official or through a faulty policy. I think if it is given to the minister in that way he will have some idea of where to check and what to check for. I have no apologies to offer for mentioning one or two matters at this time, though I am not going to discuss everything I have in mind. I understand that it is the intention to proceed as we did with the air and army estimates, and that specific questions may be discussed as we go through the estimates item by item. However, there are one or two matters of policy which I should like to bring to the minister's attention.
The first matter about which I should like to speak is the merchant marine. The minister commented on the service it is rendering, and on many occasions I have stated in the house that while we recognize the job being done by the army, the navy and the air force, and we have paid them tribute time and again, the merchant marine is a greatly neglected branch of the service, although in my opinion it is one of the most important. These men have suffered casualties; they have undergone all
	|	' _ jj| infill
kinds of hardship; yet they have not the right to wear a uniform and receive very little glory and very little recognition of the service they are performing. In my opinion they are badly treated. The minister may say this would come more properly under the Department of Transport, that he has nothing to do with the movement of these ships and very little to do with the manning pools through which the men are routed out to service. My contention is and always has been, and will continue to be, that the merchant navy should come under the direction of the Canadian navy. In the first place I believe that these boys have a right to wear a uniform and that they should be supplied with uniforms by the government as uniforms are supplied to other branches of the service. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) rightly eulogized the work of the navy in connection with convoying, but he failed to mention the boys who are taking the real licking, the boys on these old ships with very little means of protection. If a ship in a convoy gets knocked off, the others carry on and that ship is left to struggle on alone. These men are taking the real chances, the real lickings; they are suffering the real hardships, and in my opinion they should be handled exactly as the other services are handled in this country.
What happens to one of these boys if he becomes a casualty? I said that perhaps the shortest and best way to bring a matter to the minister's attention was to cite an example, and I have a case here of a boy who served two years in the merchant marine. He went all over the world, then came back to Halifax and was discharged from his ship, suffering from a mental condition no doubt brought on by his service. He wandered around Halifax for a while, then was picked up and sent home to his parents in that condition. Representations have been made to everyone I could think of. The boy was placed in an ordinary mental institution in Inverness county, and not one of the best institutions in the country either; it is a place to which people are sent when all hope is gone. This boy's father has written to everyone; he has seen me, and I have written to everyone, always without results. We were given to understand that if the boy could be placed in an institution in Halifax and given the proper treatment there would be a possibility of restoring him to health, for he is only twenty years of age. But I could find no agency that would take the responsibility of guaranteeing any payment or of putting him in any institution. He is still in that place in Inverness county, and only to-day I had another letter from his father. That is pretty rotten treat-

War Appropriation-Naval Services
meat to give a boy of that age, who went to sea and took everything that came in those convoys for at least two years, during which he was at Crete and all those other places.
I leave that thought with the minister because I believe this country has a definite obligation to that boy and his parents, who are not in financial circumstances to provide treatment for him. The Department of Pensions and National Health as well as several other departments, both provincial and federal, have had this matter up for consideration without results. I believe that in a case like this a boy who has performed such services, whether in the merchant marine or in any other branch of our forces, should be provided with the medical attention necessary to restore him to his former condition of health. That is, only one case of this kind. There may be several others, and no doubt will be.
There is another matter of policy on which I should like to ask a question, and I am going to mention another case. About eighteen months ago a young man who had a special trade made application to join the navy at Halifax. He wanted to go in a specialist branch of the service, where he could make his best contribution by carrying on his own trade. Local officials were quite ready to accept him. Then, as a result of some misdemeanour committed by his parents some years ago, his application was rejected. Now he has been called up by the army. The point I wish to make is this. This man decided where he wanted to go and volunteered his services to the navy. He wanted to go into the branch of the service where he could make his best contribution, where it would take the least training to qualify him to make that contribution, but his application was rejected.

speechtext:
Is
that the young man my hon. friend wrote me about? My hon. friend wrote about a case similar to this; is it the same case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is right. Now this man has been called into the army. The point I am making is that he is being pulled into a branch of the service against his will. To all intents and purposes he has been forced into the service; he is a conscript, whereas months ago he volunteered his service where he could have made his maximum contribution. In the branch of the service where he is now it will take a good deal more training to qualify him than would have been the case in the navy. I do not know why that policy should prevail; if a man is acceptable in one branch of the service as far as character goes he should be acceptable in the others. If he is not suitable for one particular branch, for certain reasons, then he should not be suitable for any branch 100-84i	. '
of the service, because I put them all on the same basis when it comes to a matter of that kind. In this case I think a good deal of the country's money has been wasted. Here is a man who volunteers for the navy and who could have made his maximum contribution months ago, whereas now he is pulled in against his will and put in a branch where he will not be very well satisfied.
There is another matter I should like to call to the minister's attention, again because I think it has to do with a matter of policy.
I am not going to use any names; the minister can check these matters, because they have all been before his department in the past. There was a young man serving in the navy as a petty officer. His ship was lost and he was lost with it. His mother is seventy-three years of age. She cannot obtain an old age pension in Nova Scotia because in the days of depression, when the going was tough, she went to Detroit and lived there for a few years. Because she had spent a few years out of the province she is not now entitled to an old age pension even though she is seventy-three years of age. She has made application to the Department of Pensions and National Health for a dependents' pension because her boy who would have contributed to her support was lost at sea. The matter has not been settled; it is still in the slings. They are chasing it around.
In circumstances like this I do not think there should be any question about what should be done. In his address the minister referred to the necessity of keeping up the morale of those in the service and the obligation that we in this country have to guarantee to these boys that we are looking after their [DOT] dependents. I do not think this is a matter of policy; it is a matter of faulty administration. The boy was lost at sea and the mother has no other source of income. Things of this kind get around and relatives of boys in the service and others hear of it. Such things do not build up the morale which is so necessary.
There is another matter of policy which I should like the minister to check. I refer to the medical men who are serving at different ports under the present merchant marine-set-up. These qualified doctors have been requisitioned for service and designated to ports like Halifax, Sydney and Vancouver as port doctors. They look after all the ships coming in, including naval ships, but they are not entitled to wear a uniform. Their income is much lower than that paid to medical men in the services. Many of them have tried to transfer to the army, navy or air force-I speak from personal knowledge-but they have

War Appropriation-Naval Services
not been permitted to do so. What hurts these men most of all is the fact that they have no right to wear a service button or ribbon. Their families receive no dependents' allowance. Many of them are young men and they are making a considerable contribution, but when the war is over they are faced with the possibility of being branded as slackers. The fact is that they are carrying on one [DOT]of the toughest jobs medical men can do. They are working for fourteen hours a day and are on call at any hour of the night should a ship arrive and require examination for quarantine purposes. Most of these men are qualified for the rank of major in the army, which rank I believe is given to most medical men. This is one thing the minister should check up, because it is nothing less than an oversight to place men of this calibre in this position.
There are a number of other matters that can be discussed with the minister by way of questions, but I thought these few rambling thoughts dovetailed into the matter of policy and were in accordance with the minister's statement that matter's of this kind should be checked up in order not to leave the impression with those in the service that we were not interested in the small everyday things of life. If we take care of the small things, the large ones will take care of themselves.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, most hon. members who have taken part in this debate have been residents of the Atlantic or Pacific coasts, or of regions adjacent to large inland waters and the committee may wonder why I, a landlubber from the centre of Canada, from a point almost equidistant from the . Atlantic and the Pacific, am venturing into this debate. I do so for several reasons. Coming as I do from central Canada, I do not propose to follow the example of some of those who have spoken already and demanded special consideration for their particular harbours, nor will I attempt to vie with the hon, member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). While the debate between the hon, member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) was going on, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni turned to. me and whispered that he had a harbour at Alberni which was as expansive as the western prairies and capable of holding all the fleets in the world.
I should like to refer for a moment to the address delivered this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) and to congratulate him most sincerely upon the picture he painted of the development of the Canadian navy. I

want to commend him for the modesty he displayed in outlining those accomplishments.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). The other evening he and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) commended the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) for the achievement of the Canadian air force, and this evening the hon. member for Cape Breton South has commended the minister for the achievements of the Canadian navy. I hope these hon. members realize.that in the development of our air force and navy there has been some intensive planning, that there was somebody who directed in order to bring about this achievement, that there was somebody who planned, somebody who charted, somebody who made the blueprints. Both these hon. gentlemen belong to a group that would have the Canadian people believe they have a monopoly upon planning, blueprinting and charting courses which result in worth-while achievement.
After making a general eulogy of the minister the hon. member for Cape Breton South stated a number of specific cases. He said that in making this reference he was making no apology to the committee. However, I think the hon. member will agree that he should have apologized to the committee, because the four cases he referred to were all outside the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. He referred to the medical men on the Atlantic coast who belong to the merchant marine and serve as port doctors, and he complained of the role they were having to play in these stirring times. He said . that at some subsequent date they might be regarded as slackers. I do not think these men need have any fear. If they are performing the duties outlined by the hon. member I think they will come within the terms of that old saying "he also serves who only stands and waits".
In September, 1939, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) placed the assets, and resources of Canada at the side of. Great Britain. Since then the assets and resources of this country have been steadily, mobilized for an all-out war effort. May I remind the committee that, as an initial step in that direction, a few days after the declaration of war, when the British admiralty sent a message to the Canadian government asking it how soon the Canadian navy would be ready for convoy work, the reply was sent back "Immediately", and within six days of the declaration of war eighteen ships loaded with food and supplies left a Canadian port under convoy by the Canadian navy.

Since that day the personnel of the Canadian navy has grown forty-one times, and it is interesting to note that the greater proportion of that growth is included in the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, drawn from the four comers of Canada, from every walk and occupation in life. These young men, some 67,000 in number, have joined the Canadian navy and are serving wherever required.
I wish to thank the minister in particular for his reference to young men from the Canadian west who have joined the Canadian navy, for of the total to which I have just referred, 26,394 ratings and 1,694 officers have come from western Canada. Many of these young men, as the minister remarked this afternoon, prior to enlistment never saw a bit of water larger than a prairie slough, or a ship larger than a sailing boat on some of our smaller sheets of water. It was gratifying to us to hear the minister pay a tribute to these young men, a tribute to their courage, their alertness, their intelligence, and to the way in which they have performed their duties which were new and novel. That same tribute has been paid on a number of occasions in different parts of Canada by the minister and likewise by the Prime Minister and by many senior officers of the navy. I suggest to you, sir, that that achievement, the number of recruits who have come from western Canada, has been made possible by the enthusiasm and the steadfastness of. groups of men, who, following the last war, maintained an interest in naval matters through the operation of naval recruiting stations in different parts of Canada. In my own city of Regina we have had a naval company since the close of the last war; up to a few months ago that naval company had trained over 2,200 recruits for the Royal Canadian Navy, and these lads had later completed their special training on either the Atlantic or the Pacific. That achievement is so notable that I cannot refrain from again mentioning the names of the men who have contributed to that success. There comes to my mind Lieutenant-Commander Hall, Lieutenant-Commander Ellison, Lieutenant-Commander Grant, Lieutenant-Commander Pickersgill, all of whom are on active service in the present war; likewise Petty Officers Jeffery and Smith, who are also on active service.
I should like to commend the minister for the policy to which he referred this afternoon of naming corvettes and destroyers after important points in the Dominion of Canada. It is interesting to note that a number of corvettes have been named after Saskatchewan
cities and towns. It is a matter of regret that the corvette Weybum was lost in action. The corvette Rosthern has done excellent service, and it is a matter that should be noted, I think, that of the four submarines sunk by Canadian naval vessels unassisted, in 1943, the corvettes Moose Jaw and Regina were responsible for two of them, this being one occasion when Moose Jaw and Regina can unite in a common acclaim.
I should like to give some particulars with regard to the corvette II.M.C.S. Regina. When on duty in the Mediterranean she encountered an Italian submarine and blew her clean out of the water. At that time the ship was commanded by Lieutenant-Commander Harry Freeland, who, may I say to my friends the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) and the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier), comes from Nova Scotia. This officer has had a splendid record, having served on H.M.C.S. Assiniboine and Lord Strathcona. At the present time he is commanding officer of the frigate Outremont. The present commanding officer of II.M.C.S. Regina is Lieutenant J. W. Radford, who has had wide experience, having served on H.M.C.S. Collingwood and Orillia.
At the outbreak of- the war Canada had1 no shipbuilding industry. There were, as the minister mentioned' this afternoon, only a few ship repair yards and some 5,000 men engaged in that industry. Since that time Canada has equipped some twenty-three major shipyards and some sixty-five minor shipyards, and1 in that industry now has an investment of well over $500,000,000, employing well over 100,000 men and women, turning out ships of war and ships for the merchant navy with a total commitment approximating $1,000,000,000.
The minister mentioned this afternoon the number of corvettes that had come down the slips and the prominent part that the corvettes are playing in convoy work and in action. It may be of interest to note that the first corvette built in Canada was launched in 1739 and was contracted for by N. Lavesseur and launched at the city of Quebec. It was a corvette, then called a sloop of war, a little less in size than our frigates and having many of the features of the present-day corvette. The results that have been obtained in the shipbuilding industry, both naval and marine, is a magnificent tribute to the way in which capital and labour have worked together. It is a magnificent tribute to the way in which the management and the worker have come together in Canada's emergency to produce
